experiment.cell_state_reporting_instruction: When summarizing perturbation biology, use the quantitative group_state_summary from cell_state_analysis. If discussing lineage or cell-state composition, report the relevant state names together with their cell counts and percentages where available. Do not merely say that composition shifted. Distinguish this perturbation's state distribution from cross-target comparisons, and do not call a pathway a direct target-gene mechanism when the same signal could be explained by state-composition differences.

papers.title: The dTAG system for immediate and target-specific protein degradation.
papers.abstract: Dissection of complex biological systems requires target-specific control of the function or abundance of proteins. Genetic perturbations are limited by off-target effects, multicomponent complexity, and irreversibility. Most limiting is the requisite delay between modulation to experimental measurement. To enable the immediate and selective control of single protein abundance, we created a chemical biology system that leverages the potency of cell-permeable heterobifunctional degraders. The dTAG system pairs a novel degrader of FKBP12F36V with expression of FKBP12F36V in-frame with a protein of interest. By transgene expression or CRISPR-mediated locus-specific knock-in, we exemplify a generalizable strategy to study the immediate consequence of protein loss. Using dTAG, we observe an unexpected superior antiproliferative effect of pan-BET bromodomain degradation over selective BRD4 degradation, characterize immediate effects of KRASG12V loss on proteomic signaling, and demonstrate rapid degradation in vivo. This technology platform will confer kinetic resolution to biological investigation and provide target validation in the context of drug discovery.

papers.title: Bidirectional epigenetic editing reveals hierarchies in gene regulation.
papers.abstract: CRISPR perturbation methods are limited in their ability to study non-coding elements and genetic interactions. In this study, we developed a system for bidirectional epigenetic editing, called CRISPRai, in which we apply activating (CRISPRa) and repressive (CRISPRi) perturbations to two loci simultaneously in the same cell. We developed CRISPRai Perturb-seq by coupling dual perturbation gRNA detection with single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling study of pooled perturbations in a mixed single-cell population. We applied this platform to study the genetic interaction between two hematopoietic lineage transcription factors, SPI1 and GATA1, and discovered novel characteristics of their co-regulation on downstream target genes, including differences in SPI1 and GATA1 occupancy at genes that are regulated through different modes. We also studied the regulatory landscape of IL2 (interleukin-2) in Jurkat T cells, primary T cells and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells and elucidated mechanisms of enhancer-mediated IL2 gene regulation. CRISPRai facilitates investigation of context-specific genetic interactions, provides new insights into gene regulation and will enable exploration of non-coding disease-associated variants.

papers.title: Combinatorial single-cell CRISPR screens by direct guide RNA capture and targeted sequencing.
papers.abstract: Single-cell CRISPR screens enable the exploration of mammalian gene function and genetic regulatory networks. However, use of this technology has been limited by reliance on indirect indexing of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs). Here we present direct-capture Perturb-seq, a versatile screening approach in which expressed sgRNAs are sequenced alongside single-cell transcriptomes. Direct-capture Perturb-seq enables detection of multiple distinct sgRNA sequences from individual cells and thus allows pooled single-cell CRISPR screens to be easily paired with combinatorial perturbation libraries that contain dual-guide expression vectors. We demonstrate the utility of this approach for high-throughput investigations of genetic interactions and, leveraging this ability, dissect epistatic interactions between cholesterol biogenesis and DNA repair. Using direct capture Perturb-seq, we also show that targeting individual genes with multiple sgRNAs per cell improves efficacy of CRISPR interference and activation, facilitating the use of compact, highly active CRISPR libraries for single-cell screens. Last, we show that hybridization-based target enrichment permits sensitive, specific sequencing of informative transcripts from single-cell RNA-seq experiments.

papers.title: Rescuing dendritic cell interstitial motility sustains antitumour immunity.
papers.abstract: The dendritic cell (DC)-initiated and sustained cancer immunity cycle is indispensable for effective endogenous and therapeutically mobilized antitumour T cell responses1-8. This necessitates the continuous migration of antigen-carrying DCs from the tumour microenvironment (TME) to the tumour draining lymph nodes (tdLNs)7-13. Here, through longitudinal analysis of human and mouse tumours, we observed a progressive decrease in migratory conventional DCs (mig-cDCs) in the tdLNs during tumour progression. This decline compromised tumour-specific T cell priming and subsequent T cell supply to the TME. Using a genome-wide in vivo CRISPR screen, we identified phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) and its substrate cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) as key modulators of DC migration. Advanced tumours disrupted cGMP synthesis in DCs to decrease their motility, while PDE5 perturbation preserved the cGMP pool to restore DC migration. Mechanistically, cGMP enhanced myosin-II activity through Rho-associated factors, extending the paradigm of cGMP-regulated amoeboid migration from Dictyostelium to mammalian immune cells. Pharmacological inhibition of PDE5 using sildenafil restored mig-cDC homing to late-stage tdLNs and sustained antitumour immunity in a DC-dependent manner. Our findings bridge fundamental DC interstitial motility to antitumour immunity, revealing that its disruption in chaotic TME promotes immune evasion, and its enhancement offers a promising direction for DC-centric immunotherapy.

papers.title: Coupled Single-Cell CRISPR Screening and Epigenomic Profiling Reveals Causal Gene Regulatory Networks.
papers.abstract: Here, we present Perturb-ATAC, a method that combines multiplexed CRISPR interference or knockout with genome-wide chromatin accessibility profiling in single cells based on the simultaneous detection of CRISPR guide RNAs and open chromatin sites by assay of transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC-seq). We applied Perturb-ATAC to transcription factors (TFs), chromatin-modifying factors, and noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) in ∼4,300 single cells, encompassing more than 63 genotype-phenotype relationships. Perturb-ATAC in human B lymphocytes uncovered regulators of chromatin accessibility, TF occupancy, and nucleosome positioning and identified a hierarchy of TFs that govern B cell state, variation, and disease-associated cis-regulatory elements. Perturb-ATAC in primary human epidermal cells revealed three sequential modules of cis-elements that specify keratinocyte fate. Combinatorial deletion of all pairs of these TFs uncovered their epistatic relationships and highlighted genomic co-localization as a basis for synergistic interactions. Thus, Perturb-ATAC is a powerful strategy to dissect gene regulatory networks in development and disease.

playbook_context.context_text:
Below are the most relevant playbook rules pulled from your uploaded guidance, limited to content applicable to a perturb‑seq / scRNA‑seq CRISPR perturbation in mouse and focused on mitochondrial (OXPHOS/mitochondrial membrane), proteostasis/proteasome, and NF‑κB programs.

Assay limitations / confounders
- Dissociation / handling stress commonly drives immediate‑early genes (FOS/JUN/EGR1) and heat‑shock genes; treat these as likely artifact unless supported by orthogonal data (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ).  
- Interferon / ISG activation (IFITs, ISG15, OAS, MX) can be induced by dissociation/ambient RNA and mimic inflammatory programs (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ).  
- High mitochondrial (MT) gene fraction often signals dying/low‑quality cells (“mitochondrial inflation”) and can falsely elevate mitochondrial/OXPHOS signatures (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ; 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).  
- Cell‑type composition shifts (expansion/loss of a subtype) will create apparent pathway enrichment (e.g., extra immune cells → cytokine/NF‑κB signal) unless the change is shown inside a cell type (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ).  
- Cell cycle, ribosome/translation, and bulk stress signatures are frequent confounders in RNA readouts and can reflect fitness/toxicity rather than specific pathway activation (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Multi‑layer support = higher confidence: RNA change + matching upstream regulatory evidence (TF motif/accessibility) + protein/activity readout gives strongest causal claim (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ).  
- Within‑cell‑type vs composition: if the program changes within the same annotated cell type (per‑cell‑type DE) → likely regulatory; if driven by marker genes of a different cell type → likely composition artifact (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ).  
- Breadth and coherence: true pathway drivers usually alter many canonical members coherently (direction and kinetics). Isolated single‑gene hits or scattered enrichment are more likely reactive/noise (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).  
- Timecourse & kinetics: early, direct changes in pathway targets (minutes–hours) support driver status; late broad stress responses (apoptosis, ribosomal shutdown, UPR) often indicate secondary/reactive effects (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ).  
- Functional perturbation criterion: if orthogonal inhibition/activation of the implicated pathway removes the phenotype, classify as likely causal/driver; if not, treat as reactive or confounded (09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).  
- Uncertainty flag: conflicting layer signals (RNA up but no TF activity/protein change) → label “uncertain — needs orthogonal validation” (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ).

Tissue or cell‑type priors (what’s biologically plausible in mouse)
- Immune cells: NF‑κB / cytokines and metabolic switching (glycolysis vs OXPHOS) are plausible; strong NF‑κB without immune context is a red flag (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md ).  
- Muscle / heart / neurons: high baseline mitochondrial/OXPHOS programs are expected (mitochondrial inner membrane, respiratory chain); mitochondrial enrichment is plausible here but suspicious in unrelated cell types (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md ).  
- Proteasome / proteostasis: broadly expressed — enrichment is plausible across many tissues but interpret alongside cell state (e.g., UPR/proteotoxic stress signatures) to decide if specific or general stress (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md ; 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).  
- Rule: if a top program violates tissue plausibility (e.g., synaptic signaling in fibroblasts), default to composition/mapping artifact until validated (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md ).

Follow‑up experiments and controls (straight to the point)
- For mitochondrial / OXPHOS hits: perturb mitochondrial function (oligomycin, FCCP) and measure OCR/ECAR, cellular ATP, mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS; rescue experiments (e.g., substrate supplementation) help test causality (09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).  
- For proteasome / proteostasis hits: use proteasome inhibitors (e.g., MG132/bortezomib) and measure proteasome activity, ubiquitinated protein accumulation, and UPR markers (ATF4/CHOP) by WB/qPCR to distinguish direct proteasome perturbation from secondary stress (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).  
- For NF‑κB / inflammatory hits: perturb with IKK inhibitors or TNF stimulation and readouts should include cytokine ELISA, RELA/RELB nuclear localization, and phospho‑NF‑κB markers; loss of transcriptional phenotype on pathway inhibition supports driver status (09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).  
- Essential controls: per‑cell‑type DE analysis (to rule out composition), viability/MT fraction QC, ambient RNA checks, and multiplet filtering; include vehicle controls and unrelated sgRNA controls (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ; 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).  
- Validation strategy: require (a) per‑cell‑type reproducible transcriptional change, (b) orthogonal protein/activity assay, and (c) functional perturbation (inhibitor or genetic rescue) — only then promote “driver” classification (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).

If you want, I can:
- Map these rules directly onto your top terms/genes (Ndufs*/Sdhb, Psmd*/Psma*, NF‑κB genes) and flag per‑term which bullets apply most strongly; or  
- Produce a short validation checklist you can apply to each enriched program in your perturb‑seq output.

gpt.raw_text:
Summary
- Dataset: mouse Perturb‑seq (Giladi), 4,500 cells; lineage_state annotation.
- Composition: Car1 1,786 (39.69%), Hba‑a2 1,409 (31.31%), Gstm1 615 (13.67%), unassigned 485 (10.78%). CTRL: Car1 655/1,500 (43.67%), Hba‑a2 532 (35.47%), Gstm1 163 (10.87%), unassigned 107 (7.13%). Examples of shifts: Cebpa Car1 47.80% / Hba‑a2 46.40% (Gstm1 3.00%); Flt3 Gstm1 23.00% and unassigned 17.20%; Fcgr3 unassigned 23.40%.
- Top programs: MITO_OXPHOS (strong, coherent), UPR_PROTEOSTASIS (proteasome), cell‑cycle/replication, ribosome/translation, with a TNFR2 NF‑κB label likely arising from proteasome gene overlap.

Interpretation (cautious)
- OXPHOS/ETC: Strong enrichment across Nduf*/Cox*/Uqcr* terms (R0064, R0050, R0052, R0036, R0113). Given state mixture and scRNA mitochondrial inflation risks, treat as uncertain until within‑type changes are shown.
- Proteasome/proteostasis: Broad Psma/Psmb/Psmd/Psmc coherence (R0066, R0111, R0349, R0180, R0108); most consistent with a reactive stress/turnover program.
- NF‑κB: TNFR2 non‑canonical term (R0331) is driven by proteasome subunits, not canonical NF‑κB targets — likely annotation bleed, not true NF‑κB activation.
- DDR/p53 and cell‑cycle: Likely reactive/fitness‑linked (e.g., R0208/R0209/R0223/R0157; R0242/R0205/R0104/R0103), requiring orthogonal validation.
- Innate antiviral/helicase: Low‑level, ISG‑adjacent but sparse (R0564/R0932/R0947/R0719); likely dissociation/ambient RNA artifact.

Key confounders and limitations
- Composition differences across perturbations are substantial and can project onto pathway scores.
- High MT% and cell‑cycle modules frequently confound scRNA‑seq enrichments.
- Dissociation/ambient RNA can mimic inflammatory programs.

What to do next
- Recompute per‑cell‑type DE (Car1, Hba‑a2, Gstm1) with MT% and cell‑cycle regression; composition‑match controls.
- OXPHOS: Seahorse OCR/ECAR ± oligomycin/FCCP; Δψm (TMRE), ATP, ROS within state.
- Proteostasis: Proteasome activity ± MG132; poly‑Ub WB; ATF4/CHOP/HSPA5.
- NF‑κB: Reporter and RELA nuclear localization ± IKK inhibitor/TNF; check canonical targets within state.

Literature
- PubMed retrieval quality is low/background; use as context only, not proof (e.g., Perturb‑seq methods and related platforms: PMID: 32231336; 30580963; targeted protein degradation context: PMID: 29581585).

parsed.headline: Mitochondrial respiration and proteasome programs dominate the CRISPR Perturb‑seq RNA response in mouse (Giladi dataset), but signals are likely reactive or composition‑linked; NF‑κB labeling appears proteasome‑driven and likely artifactual.
parsed.executive_summary: Across 4,500 single cells annotated by lineage_state, composition is dominated by Car1 (1,786 cells; 39.69%) and Hba-a2 (1,409 cells; 31.31%), with Gstm1 at 615 cells (13.67%) and an unassigned pool of 485 cells (10.78%). Controls (CTRL) are Car1 655/1,500 (43.67%), Hba-a2 532 (35.47%), Gstm1 163 (10.87%), unassigned 107 (7.13%). Several perturbations show different mixtures: for example, Cebpa has Car1 239/500 (47.80%) and Hba-a2 232 (46.40%) with reduced Gstm1 15 (3.00%); Flt3 shows increased Gstm1 115/500 (23.00%) and unassigned 86 (17.20%); Fcgr3 shows a high unassigned fraction 117/500 (23.40%). These mixture shifts can project strongly onto pathway enrichments. The most coherent transcriptional programs are MITO_OXPHOS (Ndufs*/Ndufv*/Cox*/Uqcr*), UPR_PROTEOSTASIS (Psma*/Psmb*/Psmd*/Psmc*), and generic cell‑cycle/translation modules. An NF‑κB label appears via a TNFR2 Reactome term but is driven by proteasome subunits, not classical NF‑κB targets. Consistent with the playbook, we treat: (a) OXPHOS as uncertain without per‑cell‑type confirmation (mitochondrial inflation and composition are key risks); (b) proteasome/proteostasis as likely reactive stress; (c) NF‑κB as likely an annotation artifact; and (d) DDR/p53 and cell‑cycle terms as likely reactive or fitness‑linked. PubMed retrieval here is background‑level; no direct causal literature applies. Follow‑up should prioritize per‑cell‑type DE controlling for state composition and orthogonal functional assays (Seahorse OCR/ECAR for OXPHOS; proteasome activity and poly‑Ub for UPR/PROTEOSTASIS), with pathway perturbation/rescue to test causality.

claims.rationale: Multiple high‑specificity terms for electron transport and inner membrane are top‑ranked with large gene overlaps (e.g., OXPHOS, complex I/ETC, inner membrane). parsed.markdown_report:
Summary
- Dataset: mouse Perturb‑seq (Giladi), 4,500 cells; lineage_state annotation.
- Composition: Car1 1,786 (39.69%), Hba‑a2 1,409 (31.31%), Gstm1 615 (13.67%), unassigned 485 (10.78%). CTRL: Car1 655/1,500 (43.67%), Hba‑a2 532 (35.47%), Gstm1 163 (10.87%), unassigned 107 (7.13%). Examples of shifts: Cebpa Car1 47.80% / Hba‑a2 46.40% (Gstm1 3.00%); Flt3 Gstm1 23.00% and unassigned 17.20%; Fcgr3 unassigned 23.40%.
- Top programs: MITO_OXPHOS (strong, coherent), UPR_PROTEOSTASIS (proteasome), cell‑cycle/replication, ribosome/translation, with a TNFR2 NF‑κB label likely arising from proteasome gene overlap.

Interpretation (cautious)
- OXPHOS/ETC: Strong enrichment across Nduf*/Cox*/Uqcr* terms (R0064, R0050, R0052, R0036, R0113). Given state mixture and scRNA mitochondrial inflation risks, treat as uncertain until within‑type changes are shown.
- Proteasome/proteostasis: Broad Psma/Psmb/Psmd/Psmc coherence (R0066, R0111, R0349, R0180, R0108); most consistent with a reactive stress/turnover program.
- NF‑κB: TNFR2 non‑canonical term (R0331) is driven by proteasome subunits, not canonical NF‑κB targets — likely annotation bleed, not true NF‑κB activation.
- DDR/p53 and cell‑cycle: Likely reactive/fitness‑linked (e.g., R0208/R0209/R0223/R0157; R0242/R0205/R0104/R0103), requiring orthogonal validation.
- Innate antiviral/helicase: Low‑level, ISG‑adjacent but sparse (R0564/R0932/R0947/R0719); likely dissociation/ambient RNA artifact.

Key confounders and limitations
- Composition differences across perturbations are substantial and can project onto pathway scores.
- High MT% and cell‑cycle modules frequently confound scRNA‑seq enrichments.

papers.title: The dTAG system for immediate and target-specific protein degradation.
papers.abstract: Dissection of complex biological systems requires target-specific control of the function or abundance of proteins. Genetic perturbations are limited by off-target effects, multicomponent complexity, and irreversibility. Most limiting is the requisite delay between modulation to experimental measurement. To enable the immediate and selective control of single protein abundance, we created a chemical biology system that leverages the potency of cell-permeable heterobifunctional degraders. The dTAG system pairs a novel degrader of FKBP12F36V with expression of FKBP12F36V in-frame with a protein of interest. By transgene expression or CRISPR-mediated locus-specific knock-in, we exemplify a generalizable strategy to study the immediate consequence of protein loss. Using dTAG, we observe an unexpected superior antiproliferative effect of pan-BET bromodomain degradation over selective BRD4 degradation, characterize immediate effects of KRASG12V loss on proteomic signaling, and demonstrate rapid degradation in vivo. This technology platform will confer kinetic resolution to biological investigation and provide target validation in the context of drug discovery.

papers.title: Bidirectional epigenetic editing reveals hierarchies in gene regulation.
papers.abstract: CRISPR perturbation methods are limited in their ability to study non-coding elements and genetic interactions. In this study, we developed a system for bidirectional epigenetic editing, called CRISPRai, in which we apply activating (CRISPRa) and repressive (CRISPRi) perturbations to two loci simultaneously in the same cell. We developed CRISPRai Perturb-seq by coupling dual perturbation gRNA detection with single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling study of pooled perturbations in a mixed single-cell population. We applied this platform to study the genetic interaction between two hematopoietic lineage transcription factors, SPI1 and GATA1, and discovered novel characteristics of their co-regulation on downstream target genes, including differences in SPI1 and GATA1 occupancy at genes that are regulated through different modes. We also studied the regulatory landscape of IL2 (interleukin-2) in Jurkat T cells, primary T cells and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells and elucidated mechanisms of enhancer-mediated IL2 gene regulation. CRISPRai facilitates investigation of context-specific genetic interactions, provides new insights into gene regulation and will enable exploration of non-coding disease-associated variants.

papers.title: Combinatorial single-cell CRISPR screens by direct guide RNA capture and targeted sequencing.
papers.abstract: Single-cell CRISPR screens enable the exploration of mammalian gene function and genetic regulatory networks. However, use of this technology has been limited by reliance on indirect indexing of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs). Here we present direct-capture Perturb-seq, a versatile screening approach in which expressed sgRNAs are sequenced alongside single-cell transcriptomes. Direct-capture Perturb-seq enables detection of multiple distinct sgRNA sequences from individual cells and thus allows pooled single-cell CRISPR screens to be easily paired with combinatorial perturbation libraries that contain dual-guide expression vectors. We demonstrate the utility of this approach for high-throughput investigations of genetic interactions and, leveraging this ability, dissect epistatic interactions between cholesterol biogenesis and DNA repair. Using direct capture Perturb-seq, we also show that targeting individual genes with multiple sgRNAs per cell improves efficacy of CRISPR interference and activation, facilitating the use of compact, highly active CRISPR libraries for single-cell screens. Last, we show that hybridization-based target enrichment permits sensitive, specific sequencing of informative transcripts from single-cell RNA-seq experiments.

papers.title: Rescuing dendritic cell interstitial motility sustains antitumour immunity.
papers.abstract: The dendritic cell (DC)-initiated and sustained cancer immunity cycle is indispensable for effective endogenous and therapeutically mobilized antitumour T cell responses1-8. This necessitates the continuous migration of antigen-carrying DCs from the tumour microenvironment (TME) to the tumour draining lymph nodes (tdLNs)7-13. Here, through longitudinal analysis of human and mouse tumours, we observed a progressive decrease in migratory conventional DCs (mig-cDCs) in the tdLNs during tumour progression. This decline compromised tumour-specific T cell priming and subsequent T cell supply to the TME. Using a genome-wide in vivo CRISPR screen, we identified phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) and its substrate cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) as key modulators of DC migration. Advanced tumours disrupted cGMP synthesis in DCs to decrease their motility, while PDE5 perturbation preserved the cGMP pool to restore DC migration. Mechanistically, cGMP enhanced myosin-II activity through Rho-associated factors, extending the paradigm of cGMP-regulated amoeboid migration from Dictyostelium to mammalian immune cells. Pharmacological inhibition of PDE5 using sildenafil restored mig-cDC homing to late-stage tdLNs and sustained antitumour immunity in a DC-dependent manner. Our findings bridge fundamental DC interstitial motility to antitumour immunity, revealing that its disruption in chaotic TME promotes immune evasion, and its enhancement offers a promising direction for DC-centric immunotherapy.

papers.title: Coupled Single-Cell CRISPR Screening and Epigenomic Profiling Reveals Causal Gene Regulatory Networks.
papers.abstract: Here, we present Perturb-ATAC, a method that combines multiplexed CRISPR interference or knockout with genome-wide chromatin accessibility profiling in single cells based on the simultaneous detection of CRISPR guide RNAs and open chromatin sites by assay of transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC-seq). We applied Perturb-ATAC to transcription factors (TFs), chromatin-modifying factors, and noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) in ∼4,300 single cells, encompassing more than 63 genotype-phenotype relationships. Perturb-ATAC in human B lymphocytes uncovered regulators of chromatin accessibility, TF occupancy, and nucleosome positioning and identified a hierarchy of TFs that govern B cell state, variation, and disease-associated cis-regulatory elements. Perturb-ATAC in primary human epidermal cells revealed three sequential modules of cis-elements that specify keratinocyte fate. Combinatorial deletion of all pairs of these TFs uncovered their epistatic relationships and highlighted genomic co-localization as a basis for synergistic interactions. Thus, Perturb-ATAC is a powerful strategy to dissect gene regulatory networks in development and disease.

playbook_context.context_text:
Below are the most relevant playbook rules pulled from your uploaded guidance, limited to content applicable to a perturb‑seq / scRNA‑seq CRISPR perturbation in mouse and focused on mitochondrial (OXPHOS/mitochondrial membrane), proteostasis/proteasome, and NF‑κB programs.

Assay limitations / confounders
- Dissociation / handling stress commonly drives immediate‑early genes (FOS/JUN/EGR1) and heat‑shock genes; treat these as likely artifact unless supported by orthogonal data (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ).  
- Interferon / ISG activation (IFITs, ISG15, OAS, MX) can be induced by dissociation/ambient RNA and mimic inflammatory programs (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ).  
- High mitochondrial (MT) gene fraction often signals dying/low‑quality cells (“mitochondrial inflation”) and can falsely elevate mitochondrial/OXPHOS signatures (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ; 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).  
- Cell‑type composition shifts (expansion/loss of a subtype) will create apparent pathway enrichment (e.g., extra immune cells → cytokine/NF‑κB signal) unless the change is shown inside a cell type (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ).  
- Cell cycle, ribosome/translation, and bulk stress signatures are frequent confounders in RNA readouts and can reflect fitness/toxicity rather than specific pathway activation (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Multi‑layer support = higher confidence: RNA change + matching upstream regulatory evidence (TF motif/accessibility) + protein/activity readout gives strongest causal claim (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ).  
- Within‑cell‑type vs composition: if the program changes within the same annotated cell type (per‑cell‑type DE) → likely regulatory; if driven by marker genes of a different cell type → likely composition artifact (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ).  
- Breadth and coherence: true pathway drivers usually alter many canonical members coherently (direction and kinetics). Isolated single‑gene hits or scattered enrichment are more likely reactive/noise (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).  
- Timecourse & kinetics: early, direct changes in pathway targets (minutes–hours) support driver status; late broad stress responses (apoptosis, ribosomal shutdown, UPR) often indicate secondary/reactive effects (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ).  
- Functional perturbation criterion: if orthogonal inhibition/activation of the implicated pathway removes the phenotype, classify as likely causal/driver; if not, treat as reactive or confounded (09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).  
- Uncertainty flag: conflicting layer signals (RNA up but no TF activity/protein change) → label “uncertain — needs orthogonal validation” (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ).

Tissue or cell‑type priors (what’s biologically plausible in mouse)
- Immune cells: NF‑κB / cytokines and metabolic switching (glycolysis vs OXPHOS) are plausible; strong NF‑κB without immune context is a red flag (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md ).  
- Muscle / heart / neurons: high baseline mitochondrial/OXPHOS programs are expected (mitochondrial inner membrane, respiratory chain); mitochondrial enrichment is plausible here but suspicious in unrelated cell types (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md ).  
- Proteasome / proteostasis: broadly expressed — enrichment is plausible across many tissues but interpret alongside cell state (e.g., UPR/proteotoxic stress signatures) to decide if specific or general stress (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md ; 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).  
- Rule: if a top program violates tissue plausibility (e.g., synaptic signaling in fibroblasts), default to composition/mapping artifact until validated (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md ).

Follow‑up experiments and controls (straight to the point)
- For mitochondrial / OXPHOS hits: perturb mitochondrial function (oligomycin, FCCP) and measure OCR/ECAR, cellular ATP, mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS; rescue experiments (e.g., substrate supplementation) help test causality (09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).  
- For proteasome / proteostasis hits: use proteasome inhibitors (e.g., MG132/bortezomib) and measure proteasome activity, ubiquitinated protein accumulation, and UPR markers (ATF4/CHOP) by WB/qPCR to distinguish direct proteasome perturbation from secondary stress (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).  
- For NF‑κB / inflammatory hits: perturb with IKK inhibitors or TNF stimulation and readouts should include cytokine ELISA, RELA/RELB nuclear localization, and phospho‑NF‑κB markers; loss of transcriptional phenotype on pathway inhibition supports driver status (09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).  
- Essential controls: per‑cell‑type DE analysis (to rule out composition), viability/MT fraction QC, ambient RNA checks, and multiplet filtering; include vehicle controls and unrelated sgRNA controls (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ; 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ).  
- Validation strategy: require (a) per‑cell‑type reproducible transcriptional change, (b) orthogonal protein/activity assay, and (c) functional perturbation (inhibitor or genetic rescue) — only then promote “driver” classification (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md ).

If you want, I can:
- Map these rules directly onto your top terms/genes (Ndufs*/Sdhb, Psmd*/Psma*, NF‑κB genes) and flag per‑term which bullets apply most strongly; or  
- Produce a short validation checklist you can apply to each enriched program in your perturb‑seq output.

display.headline: Mitochondrial respiration and proteasome programs dominate the CRISPR Perturb‑seq RNA response in mouse (Giladi dataset), but signals are likely reactive or composition‑linked; NF‑κB labeling appears proteasome‑driven and likely artifactual.
display.executive_summary: Across 4,500 single cells annotated by lineage_state, composition is dominated by Car1 (1,786 cells; 39.69%) and Hba-a2 (1,409 cells; 31.31%), with Gstm1 at 615 cells (13.67%) and an unassigned pool of 485 cells (10.78%). Controls (CTRL) are Car1 655/1,500 (43.67%), Hba-a2 532 (35.47%), Gstm1 163 (10.87%), unassigned 107 (7.13%). Several perturbations show different mixtures: for example, Cebpa has Car1 239/500 (47.80%) and Hba-a2 232 (46.40%) with reduced Gstm1 15 (3.00%); Flt3 shows increased Gstm1 115/500 (23.00%) and unassigned 86 (17.20%); Fcgr3 shows a high unassigned fraction 117/500 (23.40%). These mixture shifts can project strongly onto pathway enrichments. The most coherent transcriptional programs are MITO_OXPHOS (Ndufs*/Ndufv*/Cox*/Uqcr*), UPR_PROTEOSTASIS (Psma*/Psmb*/Psmd*/Psmc*), and generic cell‑cycle/translation modules. An NF‑κB label appears via a TNFR2 Reactome term but is driven by proteasome subunits, not classical NF‑κB targets. Consistent with the playbook, we treat: (a) OXPHOS as uncertain without per‑cell‑type confirmation (mitochondrial inflation and composition are key risks); (b) proteasome/proteostasis as likely reactive stress; (c) NF‑κB as likely an annotation artifact; and (d) DDR/p53 and cell‑cycle terms as likely reactive or fitness‑linked. PubMed retrieval here is background‑level; no direct causal literature applies. Follow‑up should prioritize per‑cell‑type DE controlling for state composition and orthogonal functional assays (Seahorse OCR/ECAR for OXPHOS; proteasome activity and poly‑Ub for UPR/PROTEOSTASIS), with pathway perturbation/rescue to test causality.

Summary
- Dataset: mouse Perturb‑seq (Giladi), 4,500 cells; lineage_state annotation.
- Composition: Car1 1,786 (39.69%), Hba‑a2 1,409 (31.31%), Gstm1 615 (13.67%), unassigned 485 (10.78%). CTRL: Car1 655/1,500 (43.67%), Hba‑a2 532 (35.47%), Gstm1 163 (10.87%), unassigned 107 (7.13%). Examples of shifts: Cebpa Car1 47.80% / Hba‑a2 46.40% (Gstm1 3.00%); Flt3 Gstm1 23.00% and unassigned 17.20%; Fcgr3 unassigned 23.40%.
- Top programs: MITO_OXPHOS (strong, coherent), UPR_PROTEOSTASIS (proteasome), cell‑cycle/replication, ribosome/translation, with a TNFR2 NF‑κB label likely arising from proteasome gene overlap.

Interpretation (cautious)
- OXPHOS/ETC: Strong enrichment across Nduf*/Cox*/Uqcr* terms (R0064, R0050, R0052, R0036, R0113). Given state mixture and scRNA mitochondrial inflation risks, treat as uncertain until within‑type changes are shown.
- Proteasome/proteostasis: Broad Psma/Psmb/Psmd/Psmc coherence (R0066, R0111, R0349, R0180, R0108); most consistent with a reactive stress/turnover program.
- NF‑κB: TNFR2 non‑canonical term (R0331) is driven by proteasome subunits, not canonical NF‑κB targets — likely annotation bleed, not true NF‑κB activation.
- DDR/p53 and cell‑cycle: Likely reactive/fitness‑linked (e.g., R0208/R0209/R0223/R0157; R0242/R0205/R0104/R0103), requiring orthogonal validation.
- Innate antiviral/helicase: Low‑level, ISG‑adjacent but sparse (R0564/R0932/R0947/R0719); likely dissociation/ambient RNA artifact.

Key confounders and limitations
- Composition differences across perturbations are substantial and can project onto pathway scores.
- High MT% and cell‑cycle modules frequently confound scRNA‑seq enrichments.
- Dissociation/ambient RNA can mimic inflammatory programs.

analysis_result.markdown_report:
Summary
- Dataset: mouse Perturb‑seq (Giladi), 4,500 cells; lineage_state annotation.
- Composition: Car1 1,786 (39.69%), Hba‑a2 1,409 (31.31%), Gstm1 615 (13.67%), unassigned 485 (10.78%). CTRL: Car1 655/1,500 (43.67%), Hba‑a2 532 (35.47%), Gstm1 163 (10.87%), unassigned 107 (7.13%). Examples of shifts: Cebpa Car1 47.80% / Hba‑a2 46.40% (Gstm1 3.00%); Flt3 Gstm1 23.00% and unassigned 17.20%; Fcgr3 unassigned 23.40%.
- Top programs: MITO_OXPHOS (strong, coherent), UPR_PROTEOSTASIS (proteasome), cell‑cycle/replication, ribosome/translation, with a TNFR2 NF‑κB label likely arising from proteasome gene overlap.

Interpretation (cautious)
- OXPHOS/ETC: Strong enrichment across Nduf*/Cox*/Uqcr* terms (R0064, R0050, R0052, R0036, R0113). Given state mixture and scRNA mitochondrial inflation risks, treat as uncertain until within‑type changes are shown.
- Proteasome/proteostasis: Broad Psma/Psmb/Psmd/Psmc coherence (R0066, R0111, R0349, R0180, R0108); most consistent with a reactive stress/turnover program.
- NF‑κB: TNFR2 non‑canonical term (R0331) is driven by proteasome subunits, not canonical NF‑κB targets — likely annotation bleed, not true NF‑κB activation.
- DDR/p53 and cell‑cycle: Likely reactive/fitness‑linked (e.g., R0208/R0209/R0223/R0157; R0242/R0205/R0104/R0103), requiring orthogonal validation.
- Innate antiviral/helicase: Low‑level, ISG‑adjacent but sparse (R0564/R0932/R0947/R0719); likely dissociation/ambient RNA artifact.

Key confounders and limitations
- Composition differences across perturbations are substantial and can project onto pathway scores.
- High MT% and cell‑cycle modules frequently confound scRNA‑seq enrichments.
- Dissociation/ambient RNA can mimic inflammatory programs.

What to do next
- Recompute per‑cell‑type DE (Car1, Hba‑a2, Gstm1) with MT% and cell‑cycle regression; composition‑match controls.
- OXPHOS: Seahorse OCR/ECAR ± oligomycin/FCCP; Δψm (TMRE), ATP, ROS within state.
- Proteostasis: Proteasome activity ± MG132; poly‑Ub WB; ATF4/CHOP/HSPA5.
- NF‑κB: Reporter and RELA nuclear localization ± IKK inhibitor/TNF; check canonical targets within state.

Literature
- PubMed retrieval quality is low/background; use as context only, not proof (e.g., Perturb‑seq methods and related platforms: PMID: 32231336; 30580963; targeted protein degradation context: PMID: 29581585).

Background single‑cell CRISPR screen papers provide technology context but not direct causality (PMID: 32231336; PMID: 30580963; PMID: 29581585).

papers.title: The dTAG system for immediate and target-specific protein degradation.
papers.abstract: Dissection of complex biological systems requires target-specific control of the function or abundance of proteins. Genetic perturbations are limited by off-target effects, multicomponent complexity, and irreversibility. Most limiting is the requisite delay between modulation to experimental measurement. To enable the immediate and selective control of single protein abundance, we created a chemical biology system that leverages the potency of cell-permeable heterobifunctional degraders. The dTAG system pairs a novel degrader of FKBP12F36V with expression of FKBP12F36V in-frame with a protein of interest. By transgene expression or CRISPR-mediated locus-specific knock-in, we exemplify a generalizable strategy to study the immediate consequence of protein loss. Using dTAG, we observe an unexpected superior antiproliferative effect of pan-BET bromodomain degradation over selective BRD4 degradation, characterize immediate effects of KRASG12V loss on proteomic signaling, and demonstrate rapid degradation in vivo. This technology platform will confer kinetic resolution to biological investigation and provide target validation in the context of drug discovery.

papers.title: Combinatorial single-cell CRISPR screens by direct guide RNA capture and targeted sequencing.
papers.abstract: Single-cell CRISPR screens enable the exploration of mammalian gene function and genetic regulatory networks. However, use of this technology has been limited by reliance on indirect indexing of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs). Here we present direct-capture Perturb-seq, a versatile screening approach in which expressed sgRNAs are sequenced alongside single-cell transcriptomes. Direct-capture Perturb-seq enables detection of multiple distinct sgRNA sequences from individual cells and thus allows pooled single-cell CRISPR screens to be easily paired with combinatorial perturbation libraries that contain dual-guide expression vectors. We demonstrate the utility of this approach for high-throughput investigations of genetic interactions and, leveraging this ability, dissect epistatic interactions between cholesterol biogenesis and DNA repair. Using direct capture Perturb-seq, we also show that targeting individual genes with multiple sgRNAs per cell improves efficacy of CRISPR interference and activation, facilitating the use of compact, highly active CRISPR libraries for single-cell screens. Last, we show that hybridization-based target enrichment permits sensitive, specific sequencing of informative transcripts from single-cell RNA-seq experiments.

papers.title: Bidirectional epigenetic editing reveals hierarchies in gene regulation.
papers.abstract: CRISPR perturbation methods are limited in their ability to study non-coding elements and genetic interactions. In this study, we developed a system for bidirectional epigenetic editing, called CRISPRai, in which we apply activating (CRISPRa) and repressive (CRISPRi) perturbations to two loci simultaneously in the same cell. We developed CRISPRai Perturb-seq by coupling dual perturbation gRNA detection with single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling study of pooled perturbations in a mixed single-cell population. We applied this platform to study the genetic interaction between two hematopoietic lineage transcription factors, SPI1 and GATA1, and discovered novel characteristics of their co-regulation on downstream target genes, including differences in SPI1 and GATA1 occupancy at genes that are regulated through different modes. We also studied the regulatory landscape of IL2 (interleukin-2) in Jurkat T cells, primary T cells and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells and elucidated mechanisms of enhancer-mediated IL2 gene regulation. CRISPRai facilitates investigation of context-specific genetic interactions, provides new insights into gene regulation and will enable exploration of non-coding disease-associated variants.

papers.title: Rescuing dendritic cell interstitial motility sustains antitumour immunity.
papers.abstract: The dendritic cell (DC)-initiated and sustained cancer immunity cycle is indispensable for effective endogenous and therapeutically mobilized antitumour T cell responses1-8. This necessitates the continuous migration of antigen-carrying DCs from the tumour microenvironment (TME) to the tumour draining lymph nodes (tdLNs)7-13. Here, through longitudinal analysis of human and mouse tumours, we observed a progressive decrease in migratory conventional DCs (mig-cDCs) in the tdLNs during tumour progression. This decline compromised tumour-specific T cell priming and subsequent T cell supply to the TME. Using a genome-wide in vivo CRISPR screen, we identified phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) and its substrate cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) as key modulators of DC migration. Advanced tumours disrupted cGMP synthesis in DCs to decrease their motility, while PDE5 perturbation preserved the cGMP pool to restore DC migration. Mechanistically, cGMP enhanced myosin-II activity through Rho-associated factors, extending the paradigm of cGMP-regulated amoeboid migration from Dictyostelium to mammalian immune cells. Pharmacological inhibition of PDE5 using sildenafil restored mig-cDC homing to late-stage tdLNs and sustained antitumour immunity in a DC-dependent manner. Our findings bridge fundamental DC interstitial motility to antitumour immunity, revealing that its disruption in chaotic TME promotes immune evasion, and its enhancement offers a promising direction for DC-centric immunotherapy.

papers.title: Coupled Single-Cell CRISPR Screening and Epigenomic Profiling Reveals Causal Gene Regulatory Networks.
papers.abstract: Here, we present Perturb-ATAC, a method that combines multiplexed CRISPR interference or knockout with genome-wide chromatin accessibility profiling in single cells based on the simultaneous detection of CRISPR guide RNAs and open chromatin sites by assay of transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC-seq). We applied Perturb-ATAC to transcription factors (TFs), chromatin-modifying factors, and noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) in ∼4,300 single cells, encompassing more than 63 genotype-phenotype relationships. Perturb-ATAC in human B lymphocytes uncovered regulators of chromatin accessibility, TF occupancy, and nucleosome positioning and identified a hierarchy of TFs that govern B cell state, variation, and disease-associated cis-regulatory elements. Perturb-ATAC in primary human epidermal cells revealed three sequential modules of cis-elements that specify keratinocyte fate. Combinatorial deletion of all pairs of these TFs uncovered their epistatic relationships and highlighted genomic co-localization as a basis for synergistic interactions. Thus, Perturb-ATAC is a powerful strategy to dissect gene regulatory networks in development and disease.

playbook_context.context_text:
Assay limitations / confounders
- Mitochondrial inflation (high MT reads) → usually indicates dying/low‑quality cells, not true OXPHOS activation; filter/report %MT and re-check per‑cell-type signals. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Dissociation / handling stress → immediate‑early and heat‑shock programs (FOS/JUN/HSPs) and IFN/ISG induction can mimic proteostasis/DDR stress. Check protocol timing and IEG/ISG markers. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Cell‑composition shifts (cell loss/expansion) produce apparent pathway enrichment (e.g., proteasome or mitochondrial programs if a high‑OXPHOS cell type expands). Always run within‑cell‑type DE and composition-aware tests. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- CRISPR/gRNA‑specific toxicity and viability selection: dropout or stress from guides often drives growth/DDR/proteostasis signatures across many guides. Monitor viability, guide counts and replicate concordance. Source: 03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md .
- Ambient RNA and doublets can spuriously inflate pathway signals (especially highly expressed genes like mitochondrial or ribosomal genes). Use ambient correction and doublet detection. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- RNA assay limitation: transcript abundance ≠ protein activity/flux (e.g., proteasome activity and OXPHOS flux need orthogonal readouts). Source: 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md .

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Basic hierarchy: multi‑layer concordance > single‑layer. RNA change supported by orthogonal functional readout (activity/phospho/OCR/proteasome assay) gives higher confidence. Source: 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md .
- Driver (likely causal) if: (a) perturbation gives consistent within‑cell‑type transcriptional changes across independent guides/replicates; (b) dose/time dependence; (c) orthogonal perturbation or inhibitor blocks phenotype; (d) functional readout altered (e.g., OCR for OXPHOS). Use rescue (re‑expression) when possible. Sources: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md , 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md .
- Reactive (downstream response) if: pathway appears broadly across many different perturbations, correlates with viability/MT fraction/IEG stress, or is limited to transcriptional changes without functional support. Source: 03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md  and 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Artifact if: enrichment tracks QC metrics (low UMIs, high %MT), is driven by cell‑type composition shifts (not within‑cell‑type), or is present only in single low‑coverage cells or in ambient RNA signatures. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Disambiguation checklist (use to classify each program): within‑cell‑type DE? multiple independent guides? timecourse/dose response? orthogonal functional change? correlated with QC/viability? concordant multi‑omics? Prioritize programs meeting >1 “driver” criterion; label others as reactive/uncertain. Sources: 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md , 03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md .

Tissue or cell‑type priors (mouse)
- Mitochondrial / OXPHOS: biologically plausible and often high in muscle, heart, and neurons; in immune cells OXPHOS shifts are plausible for metabolic switching but require cell‑type context. If enrichment violates tissue plausibility, treat cautiously. Source: 08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md .
- Proteasome / UPR / proteostasis: plausible across many cell types but strongest in secretory cells, rapidly proliferating cells, or cells undergoing proteotoxic stress; ubiquity means stronger functional validation required. Source: 08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md .
- DDR / p53 / apoptosis programs: expected in proliferating or DNA‑damaged cells (e.g., tumor or replicating populations); in non‑dividing tissues, enrichment may reflect off‑target toxicity. Source: 08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md .
- Apply the rule: if a pathway conflicts with known tissue biology, first test for composition or mapping artifacts before assigning mechanistic meaning. Source: 08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md .

Follow‑up experiments and controls (concise, prioritized)
- Validate mitochondria/OXPHOS hits:
  - Perturb: oligomycin, FCCP; Readouts: OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), ATP, mitochondrial membrane potential (TMRE), ROS. Source: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md .
  - Control: separate low‑quality/dying cells (high %MT) and re‑analyze within high‑quality subset. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Validate proteasome / UPR signals:
  - Perturb: proteasome inhibitor (e.g., bortezomib) or activator as appropriate; Readouts: proteasome activity assay, accumulation of poly‑ubiquitinated proteins, ATF4/CHOP induction for UPR. Source: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md .
- Validate DDR / apoptosis:
  - Perturb/readout: γH2AX, Annexin V / caspase assays, use caspase inhibitors to test dependence. Source: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md .
- CRISPR specificity & robustness controls:
  - Use ≥2 independent guides per target, non‑targeting controls, and rescue (cDNA) experiments; monitor guide representation and cell viability to rule out selection artifacts. Source: 03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md .
- Orthogonal and composition controls:
  - Bulk or sorted‑cell RNAseq on the affected cell type(s), flow cytometry for cell proportions, and per‑cell‑type DE to separate composition vs regulation. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Timecourse and dose:
  - Early vs late timepoints and varying perturbation strength distinguish primary (driver) vs secondary (reactive) transcriptional responses. Source: 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md .
- If inhibition/removal of the suspected pathway abolishes the phenotype → supports causality; if not, likely reactive. Source: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md .

gpt.raw_text:
# Interpretation overview
- Assay/context: mouse Perturb-seq (scRNA-seq) CRISPR perturbations; dataset: Giladi Perturb-seq; phenotype: transcriptional response.
- Top programs: MITO_OXPHOS; UPR_PROTEOSTASIS; DNA damage checkpoint; Cell-cycle; weaker NF-κB/innate-like terms.

## Cell-state composition (quantitative)
- Overall (n=4,500): Car1 1,786 (39.7%), Hba-a2 1,409 (31.3%), Gstm1 615 (13.7%), unassigned 485 (10.8%), Vpreb1 73 (1.6%), Fcnb 64 (1.4%), Ly86 23 (0.5%), Pf4 12 (0.3%), Fcrla 12 (0.3%), Prss34 7 (0.2%), Ltf 6 (0.1%), Prg2 6 (0.1%), Cd74 2 (~0.0%).
- By perturbation group (fraction within group):
  - CTRL: Car1 43.7%, Hba-a2 35.5%, Gstm1 10.9%, unassigned 7.1%, others ≤1.5%.
  - Cebpa: Car1 47.8%, Hba-a2 46.4%, Gstm1 3.0%, unassigned 2.0%.
  - Csf1r: Car1 38.4%, Hba-a2 29.4%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 10.2%, Vpreb1 4.2%.
  - Fcgr3: Car1 31.8%, Hba-a2 22.2%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 23.4%, Vpreb1 2.8%.
  - Flt3: Car1 33.8%, Gstm1 23.0%, Hba-a2 21.4%, unassigned 17.2%.
  - Irf8: Car1 39.4%, Hba-a2 27.4%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 9.6%, Vpreb1 4.0%.
  - Klf4: Car1 35.0%, Hba-a2 28.6%, Gstm1 21.2%, unassigned 13.2%.

Interpretation: several perturbations (e.g., Cebpa) have much higher Car1/Hba-a2 representation than CTRL, which can inflate mitochondrial/heme/respiration-related terms; thus composition-aware analyses are required before inferring regulation.

## Program-level interpretations (cautious)
- MITO_OXPHOS: strong enrichment across multiple terms (e.g., mitochondrial ATP synthesis coupled electron transport; respiratory chain complex) with genes including Sdhb, Ndufv1, Ndufs7, Ndufv2, Cyc1, Cox5a, Cox7a2. Given large erythroid-like fractions in some groups and lack of within-state DE/functional data, this is likely composition-driven or QC-inflated rather than a primary driver.
- UPR_PROTEOSTASIS: broad proteasome subunit upregulation (Psmc2/Psma/Psmb/Psmd) consistent with generic stress or selection in CRISPR experiments; treat as reactive until functional proteostasis changes are shown.
- DDR/p53 checkpoints: enrichment likely reflects genome-editing stress and growth effects; distinguish target-driven DDR using Cas9-modality comparisons and DDR markers.
- Cell-cycle: enriched and flagged as potential artifact; likely reflects proliferative-subset differences; validate with cell-cycle regression and Ki-67/EdU.
- NF-κB (non-canonical) and weak innate/RNA-binding signals: low confidence; validate with pathway reporters and cytokine/ISG profiling.

## Assay limitations and confounders
- High %MT reads and low-quality cells can mimic OXPHOS activation; dissociation stress can induce IEG/HSP/IFN-like programs; CRISPR guide toxicity and viability selection can elevate growth/DDR/proteostasis signatures; ambient RNA/doublets can inflate abundant transcripts; RNA levels may not reflect activity/flux.

## Minimal validation plan (prioritized)
1) Within-state DE with composition-aware modeling; exclude high-%MT cells and regress cell-cycle; confirm whether OXPHOS and proteasome signals persist within states.
2) Functional assays: Seahorse OCR/ATP and TMRE/ROS in sorted matched states; proteasome activity and UPR markers (ATF4/CHOP).
3) Specificity: ≥2 independent guides per target, non-targeting controls, and rescue by re-expression.
4) Editing modality control: compare nuclease Cas9 vs base editor/dCas9 to parse DDR contributions.

## Literature context
PubMed retrieval was low-specificity and used as background only; general single-cell CRISPR technologies are consistent with the experimental setup (e.g., direct-capture Perturb-seq and Perturb-ATAC; PMID: 32231336, 30580963) but do not provide direct mechanistic support for the enriched programs here.

parsed.headline: Perturb-seq CRISPR perturbations in mouse hematopoietic-lineage cells show strong mitochondrial OXPHOS and proteasome/UPR transcriptional programs, with evidence pointing to composition and stress-related confounding rather than direct target-driven regulation
parsed.executive_summary: Across 4,500 single cells (Giladi Perturb‑seq), the dominant annotated states are Car1 (1,786; 39.7%), Hba-a2 (1,409; 31.3%), Gstm1 (615; 13.7%), and unassigned (485; 10.8%). State distributions differ by perturbation: for example, CTRL is 43.7% Car1 and 35.5% Hba-a2, whereas Cebpa is 47.8% Car1 and 46.4% Hba-a2 with a marked reduction of Gstm1 (3.0% vs 10.9% in CTRL). The top enriched programs are MITO_OXPHOS and UPR_PROTEOSTASIS, with additional DNA damage checkpoint, cell‑cycle, and weak NF‑kB/innate signatures. Given the pronounced lineage composition differences and known scRNA‑seq/CRISPR confounders, these programs are most consistent with reactive or composition‑driven signals rather than primary, target‑specific drivers. We outline focused, within‑cell‑type and orthogonal functional validations to test causality and to separate regulation from composition and QC artifacts.

claims.claim: A mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) transcriptional program is enriched but is likely confounded by lineage composition differences rather than being a primary, target-specific effect.
claims.rationale: Multiple high-confidence OXPHOS/ETC terms are enriched (e.g., mitochondrial ATP synthesis coupled electron transport; respiratory chain complexes) with repeated involvement of complex I/III/IV genes. However, perturbations show large differences in erythroid-like states (e.g., Cebpa: Car1 47.8%, Hba-a2 46.4%) relative to CTRL (Car1 43.7%, Hba-a2 35.5%), which can inflate mitochondrial pathway scores without within-state regulation. No orthogonal metabolic readouts are provided, and OXPHOS shifts are common artifacts of composition or QC differences in scRNA-seq.
supporting_terms: mitochondrial ATP synthesis coupled electron transport (GO:BP)
confounders: Cell-type composition differences across perturbations (elevated Car1/Hba-a2 in some groups)
High mitochondrial read fraction inflating OXPHOS signatures
Ambient RNA/doublets elevating abundant mitochondrial/ribosomal transcripts
CRISPR guide toxicity and selection favoring metabolic rewiring

validation.purpose: Rule out mitochondrial inflation and low-quality-cell artifacts

validation.control: Non-targeting guides; rescue by re-expression of target cDNA
validation.expected_result_if_causal: Directionally consistent change in OCR/ATP aligned with scRNA OXPHOS shifts
validation.purpose: Test whether transcriptional OXPHOS signals reflect functional mitochondrial changes

claims.claim: A proteasome/UPR-proteostasis program is activated and is most consistent with a reactive stress response to CRISPR perturbation rather than a specific target-driven mechanism.

No orthogonal proteostasis readouts are provided, and signals appear generic rather than target-specific.

Transcript–protein disconnect (UPR/proteasome activity not measured)

papers.title: The dTAG system for immediate and target-specific protein degradation.
papers.abstract: Dissection of complex biological systems requires target-specific control of the function or abundance of proteins. Genetic perturbations are limited by off-target effects, multicomponent complexity, and irreversibility. Most limiting is the requisite delay between modulation to experimental measurement. To enable the immediate and selective control of single protein abundance, we created a chemical biology system that leverages the potency of cell-permeable heterobifunctional degraders. The dTAG system pairs a novel degrader of FKBP12F36V with expression of FKBP12F36V in-frame with a protein of interest. By transgene expression or CRISPR-mediated locus-specific knock-in, we exemplify a generalizable strategy to study the immediate consequence of protein loss. Using dTAG, we observe an unexpected superior antiproliferative effect of pan-BET bromodomain degradation over selective BRD4 degradation, characterize immediate effects of KRASG12V loss on proteomic signaling, and demonstrate rapid degradation in vivo. This technology platform will confer kinetic resolution to biological investigation and provide target validation in the context of drug discovery.

papers.title: Combinatorial single-cell CRISPR screens by direct guide RNA capture and targeted sequencing.
papers.abstract: Single-cell CRISPR screens enable the exploration of mammalian gene function and genetic regulatory networks. However, use of this technology has been limited by reliance on indirect indexing of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs). Here we present direct-capture Perturb-seq, a versatile screening approach in which expressed sgRNAs are sequenced alongside single-cell transcriptomes. Direct-capture Perturb-seq enables detection of multiple distinct sgRNA sequences from individual cells and thus allows pooled single-cell CRISPR screens to be easily paired with combinatorial perturbation libraries that contain dual-guide expression vectors. We demonstrate the utility of this approach for high-throughput investigations of genetic interactions and, leveraging this ability, dissect epistatic interactions between cholesterol biogenesis and DNA repair. Using direct capture Perturb-seq, we also show that targeting individual genes with multiple sgRNAs per cell improves efficacy of CRISPR interference and activation, facilitating the use of compact, highly active CRISPR libraries for single-cell screens. Last, we show that hybridization-based target enrichment permits sensitive, specific sequencing of informative transcripts from single-cell RNA-seq experiments.

papers.title: Bidirectional epigenetic editing reveals hierarchies in gene regulation.
papers.abstract: CRISPR perturbation methods are limited in their ability to study non-coding elements and genetic interactions. In this study, we developed a system for bidirectional epigenetic editing, called CRISPRai, in which we apply activating (CRISPRa) and repressive (CRISPRi) perturbations to two loci simultaneously in the same cell. We developed CRISPRai Perturb-seq by coupling dual perturbation gRNA detection with single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling study of pooled perturbations in a mixed single-cell population. We applied this platform to study the genetic interaction between two hematopoietic lineage transcription factors, SPI1 and GATA1, and discovered novel characteristics of their co-regulation on downstream target genes, including differences in SPI1 and GATA1 occupancy at genes that are regulated through different modes. We also studied the regulatory landscape of IL2 (interleukin-2) in Jurkat T cells, primary T cells and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells and elucidated mechanisms of enhancer-mediated IL2 gene regulation. CRISPRai facilitates investigation of context-specific genetic interactions, provides new insights into gene regulation and will enable exploration of non-coding disease-associated variants.

papers.title: Rescuing dendritic cell interstitial motility sustains antitumour immunity.
papers.abstract: The dendritic cell (DC)-initiated and sustained cancer immunity cycle is indispensable for effective endogenous and therapeutically mobilized antitumour T cell responses1-8. This necessitates the continuous migration of antigen-carrying DCs from the tumour microenvironment (TME) to the tumour draining lymph nodes (tdLNs)7-13. Here, through longitudinal analysis of human and mouse tumours, we observed a progressive decrease in migratory conventional DCs (mig-cDCs) in the tdLNs during tumour progression. This decline compromised tumour-specific T cell priming and subsequent T cell supply to the TME. Using a genome-wide in vivo CRISPR screen, we identified phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) and its substrate cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) as key modulators of DC migration. Advanced tumours disrupted cGMP synthesis in DCs to decrease their motility, while PDE5 perturbation preserved the cGMP pool to restore DC migration. Mechanistically, cGMP enhanced myosin-II activity through Rho-associated factors, extending the paradigm of cGMP-regulated amoeboid migration from Dictyostelium to mammalian immune cells. Pharmacological inhibition of PDE5 using sildenafil restored mig-cDC homing to late-stage tdLNs and sustained antitumour immunity in a DC-dependent manner. Our findings bridge fundamental DC interstitial motility to antitumour immunity, revealing that its disruption in chaotic TME promotes immune evasion, and its enhancement offers a promising direction for DC-centric immunotherapy.

papers.title: Coupled Single-Cell CRISPR Screening and Epigenomic Profiling Reveals Causal Gene Regulatory Networks.
papers.abstract: Here, we present Perturb-ATAC, a method that combines multiplexed CRISPR interference or knockout with genome-wide chromatin accessibility profiling in single cells based on the simultaneous detection of CRISPR guide RNAs and open chromatin sites by assay of transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC-seq). We applied Perturb-ATAC to transcription factors (TFs), chromatin-modifying factors, and noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) in ∼4,300 single cells, encompassing more than 63 genotype-phenotype relationships. Perturb-ATAC in human B lymphocytes uncovered regulators of chromatin accessibility, TF occupancy, and nucleosome positioning and identified a hierarchy of TFs that govern B cell state, variation, and disease-associated cis-regulatory elements. Perturb-ATAC in primary human epidermal cells revealed three sequential modules of cis-elements that specify keratinocyte fate. Combinatorial deletion of all pairs of these TFs uncovered their epistatic relationships and highlighted genomic co-localization as a basis for synergistic interactions. Thus, Perturb-ATAC is a powerful strategy to dissect gene regulatory networks in development and disease.

playbook_context.context_text:
Assay limitations / confounders
- Mitochondrial inflation (high MT reads) → usually indicates dying/low‑quality cells, not true OXPHOS activation; filter/report %MT and re-check per‑cell-type signals. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Dissociation / handling stress → immediate‑early and heat‑shock programs (FOS/JUN/HSPs) and IFN/ISG induction can mimic proteostasis/DDR stress. Check protocol timing and IEG/ISG markers. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Cell‑composition shifts (cell loss/expansion) produce apparent pathway enrichment (e.g., proteasome or mitochondrial programs if a high‑OXPHOS cell type expands). Always run within‑cell‑type DE and composition-aware tests. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- CRISPR/gRNA‑specific toxicity and viability selection: dropout or stress from guides often drives growth/DDR/proteostasis signatures across many guides. Monitor viability, guide counts and replicate concordance. Source: 03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md .
- Ambient RNA and doublets can spuriously inflate pathway signals (especially highly expressed genes like mitochondrial or ribosomal genes). Use ambient correction and doublet detection. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- RNA assay limitation: transcript abundance ≠ protein activity/flux (e.g., proteasome activity and OXPHOS flux need orthogonal readouts). Source: 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md .

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Basic hierarchy: multi‑layer concordance > single‑layer. RNA change supported by orthogonal functional readout (activity/phospho/OCR/proteasome assay) gives higher confidence. Source: 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md .
- Driver (likely causal) if: (a) perturbation gives consistent within‑cell‑type transcriptional changes across independent guides/replicates; (b) dose/time dependence; (c) orthogonal perturbation or inhibitor blocks phenotype; (d) functional readout altered (e.g., OCR for OXPHOS). Use rescue (re‑expression) when possible. Sources: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md , 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md .
- Reactive (downstream response) if: pathway appears broadly across many different perturbations, correlates with viability/MT fraction/IEG stress, or is limited to transcriptional changes without functional support. Source: 03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md  and 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Artifact if: enrichment tracks QC metrics (low UMIs, high %MT), is driven by cell‑type composition shifts (not within‑cell‑type), or is present only in single low‑coverage cells or in ambient RNA signatures. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Disambiguation checklist (use to classify each program): within‑cell‑type DE? multiple independent guides? timecourse/dose response? orthogonal functional change? correlated with QC/viability? concordant multi‑omics? Prioritize programs meeting >1 “driver” criterion; label others as reactive/uncertain. Sources: 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md , 03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md .

Tissue or cell‑type priors (mouse)
- Mitochondrial / OXPHOS: biologically plausible and often high in muscle, heart, and neurons; in immune cells OXPHOS shifts are plausible for metabolic switching but require cell‑type context. If enrichment violates tissue plausibility, treat cautiously. Source: 08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md .
- Proteasome / UPR / proteostasis: plausible across many cell types but strongest in secretory cells, rapidly proliferating cells, or cells undergoing proteotoxic stress; ubiquity means stronger functional validation required. Source: 08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md .
- DDR / p53 / apoptosis programs: expected in proliferating or DNA‑damaged cells (e.g., tumor or replicating populations); in non‑dividing tissues, enrichment may reflect off‑target toxicity. Source: 08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md .
- Apply the rule: if a pathway conflicts with known tissue biology, first test for composition or mapping artifacts before assigning mechanistic meaning. Source: 08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md .

Follow‑up experiments and controls (concise, prioritized)
- Validate mitochondria/OXPHOS hits:
  - Perturb: oligomycin, FCCP; Readouts: OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), ATP, mitochondrial membrane potential (TMRE), ROS. Source: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md .
  - Control: separate low‑quality/dying cells (high %MT) and re‑analyze within high‑quality subset. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Validate proteasome / UPR signals:
  - Perturb: proteasome inhibitor (e.g., bortezomib) or activator as appropriate; Readouts: proteasome activity assay, accumulation of poly‑ubiquitinated proteins, ATF4/CHOP induction for UPR. Source: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md .
- Validate DDR / apoptosis:
  - Perturb/readout: γH2AX, Annexin V / caspase assays, use caspase inhibitors to test dependence. Source: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md .
- CRISPR specificity & robustness controls:
  - Use ≥2 independent guides per target, non‑targeting controls, and rescue (cDNA) experiments; monitor guide representation and cell viability to rule out selection artifacts. Source: 03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md .
- Orthogonal and composition controls:
  - Bulk or sorted‑cell RNAseq on the affected cell type(s), flow cytometry for cell proportions, and per‑cell‑type DE to separate composition vs regulation. Source: 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md .
- Timecourse and dose:
  - Early vs late timepoints and varying perturbation strength distinguish primary (driver) vs secondary (reactive) transcriptional responses. Source: 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md .
- If inhibition/removal of the suspected pathway abolishes the phenotype → supports causality; if not, likely reactive. Source: 09_followup_experiment_menu.md .

If you want, I can: (A) map these rules specifically to your gene list (Sdhb, Ndufv1, Ndufs7, Psmc2, Psma5, Psmb3) and suggest a minimal validation experiment plan (order of priority + expected positive/negative controls), or (B) produce a short checklist you can paste into your analysis pipeline for automated flagging. Which would you prefer?

display.headline: Perturb-seq CRISPR perturbations in mouse hematopoietic-lineage cells show strong mitochondrial OXPHOS and proteasome/UPR transcriptional programs, with evidence pointing to composition and stress-related confounding rather than direct target-driven regulation
display.executive_summary: Across 4,500 single cells (Giladi Perturb‑seq), the dominant annotated states are Car1 (1,786; 39.7%), Hba-a2 (1,409; 31.3%), Gstm1 (615; 13.7%), and unassigned (485; 10.8%). State distributions differ by perturbation: for example, CTRL is 43.7% Car1 and 35.5% Hba-a2, whereas Cebpa is 47.8% Car1 and 46.4% Hba-a2 with a marked reduction of Gstm1 (3.0% vs 10.9% in CTRL). The top enriched programs are MITO_OXPHOS and UPR_PROTEOSTASIS, with additional DNA damage checkpoint, cell‑cycle, and weak NF‑kB/innate signatures. Given the pronounced lineage composition differences and known scRNA‑seq/CRISPR confounders, these programs are most consistent with reactive or composition‑driven signals rather than primary, target‑specific drivers. We outline focused, within‑cell‑type and orthogonal functional validations to test causality and to separate regulation from composition and QC artifacts.

display.raw_text:
# Interpretation overview
- Assay/context: mouse Perturb-seq (scRNA-seq) CRISPR perturbations; dataset: Giladi Perturb-seq; phenotype: transcriptional response.
- Top programs: MITO_OXPHOS; UPR_PROTEOSTASIS; DNA damage checkpoint; Cell-cycle; weaker NF-κB/innate-like terms.

## Cell-state composition (quantitative)
- Overall (n=4,500): Car1 1,786 (39.7%), Hba-a2 1,409 (31.3%), Gstm1 615 (13.7%), unassigned 485 (10.8%), Vpreb1 73 (1.6%), Fcnb 64 (1.4%), Ly86 23 (0.5%), Pf4 12 (0.3%), Fcrla 12 (0.3%), Prss34 7 (0.2%), Ltf 6 (0.1%), Prg2 6 (0.1%), Cd74 2 (~0.0%).
- By perturbation group (fraction within group):
  - CTRL: Car1 43.7%, Hba-a2 35.5%, Gstm1 10.9%, unassigned 7.1%, others ≤1.5%.
  - Cebpa: Car1 47.8%, Hba-a2 46.4%, Gstm1 3.0%, unassigned 2.0%.
  - Csf1r: Car1 38.4%, Hba-a2 29.4%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 10.2%, Vpreb1 4.2%.
  - Fcgr3: Car1 31.8%, Hba-a2 22.2%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 23.4%, Vpreb1 2.8%.
  - Flt3: Car1 33.8%, Gstm1 23.0%, Hba-a2 21.4%, unassigned 17.2%.
  - Irf8: Car1 39.4%, Hba-a2 27.4%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 9.6%, Vpreb1 4.0%.
  - Klf4: Car1 35.0%, Hba-a2 28.6%, Gstm1 21.2%, unassigned 13.2%.

Interpretation: several perturbations (e.g., Cebpa) have much higher Car1/Hba-a2 representation than CTRL, which can inflate mitochondrial/heme/respiration-related terms; thus composition-aware analyses are required before inferring regulation.

## Program-level interpretations (cautious)
- MITO_OXPHOS: strong enrichment across multiple terms (e.g., mitochondrial ATP synthesis coupled electron transport; respiratory chain complex) with genes including Sdhb, Ndufv1, Ndufs7, Ndufv2, Cyc1, Cox5a, Cox7a2. Given large erythroid-like fractions in some groups and lack of within-state DE/functional data, this is likely composition-driven or QC-inflated rather than a primary driver.
- UPR_PROTEOSTASIS: broad proteasome subunit upregulation (Psmc2/Psma/Psmb/Psmd) consistent with generic stress or selection in CRISPR experiments; treat as reactive until functional proteostasis changes are shown.
- DDR/p53 checkpoints: enrichment likely reflects genome-editing stress and growth effects; distinguish target-driven DDR using Cas9-modality comparisons and DDR markers.
- Cell-cycle: enriched and flagged as potential artifact; likely reflects proliferative-subset differences; validate with cell-cycle regression and Ki-67/EdU.
- NF-κB (non-canonical) and weak innate/RNA-binding signals: low confidence; validate with pathway reporters and cytokine/ISG profiling.

## Assay limitations and confounders
- High %MT reads and low-quality cells can mimic OXPHOS activation; dissociation stress can induce IEG/HSP/IFN-like programs; CRISPR guide toxicity and viability selection can elevate growth/DDR/proteostasis signatures; ambient RNA/doublets can inflate abundant transcripts; RNA levels may not reflect activity/flux.

## Minimal validation plan (prioritized)
1) Within-state DE with composition-aware modeling; exclude high-%MT cells and regress cell-cycle; confirm whether OXPHOS and proteasome signals persist within states.
2) Functional assays: Seahorse OCR/ATP and TMRE/ROS in sorted matched states; proteasome activity and UPR markers (ATF4/CHOP).
3) Specificity: ≥2 independent guides per target, non-targeting controls, and rescue by re-expression.
4) Editing modality control: compare nuclease Cas9 vs base editor/dCas9 to parse DDR contributions.

## Literature context
PubMed retrieval was low-specificity and used as background only; general single-cell CRISPR technologies are consistent with the experimental setup (e.g., direct-capture Perturb-seq and Perturb-ATAC; PMID: 32231336, 30580963) but do not provide direct mechanistic support for the enriched programs here.

No orthogonal proteostasis readouts are provided, and signals appear generic rather than target-specific.

analysis_result.markdown_report:
# Interpretation overview
- Assay/context: mouse Perturb-seq (scRNA-seq) CRISPR perturbations; dataset: Giladi Perturb-seq; phenotype: transcriptional response.
- Top programs: MITO_OXPHOS; UPR_PROTEOSTASIS; DNA damage checkpoint; Cell-cycle; weaker NF-κB/innate-like terms.

## Cell-state composition (quantitative)
- Overall (n=4,500): Car1 1,786 (39.7%), Hba-a2 1,409 (31.3%), Gstm1 615 (13.7%), unassigned 485 (10.8%), Vpreb1 73 (1.6%), Fcnb 64 (1.4%), Ly86 23 (0.5%), Pf4 12 (0.3%), Fcrla 12 (0.3%), Prss34 7 (0.2%), Ltf 6 (0.1%), Prg2 6 (0.1%), Cd74 2 (~0.0%).
- By perturbation group (fraction within group):
  - CTRL: Car1 43.7%, Hba-a2 35.5%, Gstm1 10.9%, unassigned 7.1%, others ≤1.5%.
  - Cebpa: Car1 47.8%, Hba-a2 46.4%, Gstm1 3.0%, unassigned 2.0%.
  - Csf1r: Car1 38.4%, Hba-a2 29.4%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 10.2%, Vpreb1 4.2%.
  - Fcgr3: Car1 31.8%, Hba-a2 22.2%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 23.4%, Vpreb1 2.8%.
  - Flt3: Car1 33.8%, Gstm1 23.0%, Hba-a2 21.4%, unassigned 17.2%.
  - Irf8: Car1 39.4%, Hba-a2 27.4%, Gstm1 14.4%, unassigned 9.6%, Vpreb1 4.0%.
  - Klf4: Car1 35.0%, Hba-a2 28.6%, Gstm1 21.2%, unassigned 13.2%.

Interpretation: several perturbations (e.g., Cebpa) have much higher Car1/Hba-a2 representation than CTRL, which can inflate mitochondrial/heme/respiration-related terms; thus composition-aware analyses are required before inferring regulation.

## Program-level interpretations (cautious)
- MITO_OXPHOS: strong enrichment across multiple terms (e.g., mitochondrial ATP synthesis coupled electron transport; respiratory chain complex) with genes including Sdhb, Ndufv1, Ndufs7, Ndufv2, Cyc1, Cox5a, Cox7a2. Given large erythroid-like fractions in some groups and lack of within-state DE/functional data, this is likely composition-driven or QC-inflated rather than a primary driver.
- UPR_PROTEOSTASIS: broad proteasome subunit upregulation (Psmc2/Psma/Psmb/Psmd) consistent with generic stress or selection in CRISPR experiments; treat as reactive until functional proteostasis changes are shown.
- DDR/p53 checkpoints: enrichment likely reflects genome-editing stress and growth effects; distinguish target-driven DDR using Cas9-modality comparisons and DDR markers.
- Cell-cycle: enriched and flagged as potential artifact; likely reflects proliferative-subset differences; validate with cell-cycle regression and Ki-67/EdU.
- NF-κB (non-canonical) and weak innate/RNA-binding signals: low confidence; validate with pathway reporters and cytokine/ISG profiling.

## Assay limitations and confounders
- High %MT reads and low-quality cells can mimic OXPHOS activation; dissociation stress can induce IEG/HSP/IFN-like programs; CRISPR guide toxicity and viability selection can elevate growth/DDR/proteostasis signatures; ambient RNA/doublets can inflate abundant transcripts; RNA levels may not reflect activity/flux.

## Minimal validation plan (prioritized)
1) Within-state DE with composition-aware modeling; exclude high-%MT cells and regress cell-cycle; confirm whether OXPHOS and proteasome signals persist within states.
2) Functional assays: Seahorse OCR/ATP and TMRE/ROS in sorted matched states; proteasome activity and UPR markers (ATF4/CHOP).
3) Specificity: ≥2 independent guides per target, non-targeting controls, and rescue by re-expression.
4) Editing modality control: compare nuclease Cas9 vs base editor/dCas9 to parse DDR contributions.

## Literature context
PubMed retrieval was low-specificity and used as background only; general single-cell CRISPR technologies are consistent with the experimental setup (e.g., direct-capture Perturb-seq and Perturb-ATAC; PMID: 32231336, 30580963) but do not provide direct mechanistic support for the enriched programs here.
