papers.title: The dTAG system for immediate and target-specific protein degradation.
papers.abstract: Dissection of complex biological systems requires target-specific control of the function or abundance of proteins. Genetic perturbations are limited by off-target effects, multicomponent complexity, and irreversibility. Most limiting is the requisite delay between modulation to experimental measurement. To enable the immediate and selective control of single protein abundance, we created a chemical biology system that leverages the potency of cell-permeable heterobifunctional degraders. The dTAG system pairs a novel degrader of FKBP12F36V with expression of FKBP12F36V in-frame with a protein of interest. By transgene expression or CRISPR-mediated locus-specific knock-in, we exemplify a generalizable strategy to study the immediate consequence of protein loss. Using dTAG, we observe an unexpected superior antiproliferative effect of pan-BET bromodomain degradation over selective BRD4 degradation, characterize immediate effects of KRASG12V loss on proteomic signaling, and demonstrate rapid degradation in vivo. This technology platform will confer kinetic resolution to biological investigation and provide target validation in the context of drug discovery.

papers.title: Bidirectional epigenetic editing reveals hierarchies in gene regulation.
papers.abstract: CRISPR perturbation methods are limited in their ability to study non-coding elements and genetic interactions. In this study, we developed a system for bidirectional epigenetic editing, called CRISPRai, in which we apply activating (CRISPRa) and repressive (CRISPRi) perturbations to two loci simultaneously in the same cell. We developed CRISPRai Perturb-seq by coupling dual perturbation gRNA detection with single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling study of pooled perturbations in a mixed single-cell population. We applied this platform to study the genetic interaction between two hematopoietic lineage transcription factors, SPI1 and GATA1, and discovered novel characteristics of their co-regulation on downstream target genes, including differences in SPI1 and GATA1 occupancy at genes that are regulated through different modes. We also studied the regulatory landscape of IL2 (interleukin-2) in Jurkat T cells, primary T cells and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells and elucidated mechanisms of enhancer-mediated IL2 gene regulation. CRISPRai facilitates investigation of context-specific genetic interactions, provides new insights into gene regulation and will enable exploration of non-coding disease-associated variants.

papers.title: Combinatorial single-cell CRISPR screens by direct guide RNA capture and targeted sequencing.
papers.abstract: Single-cell CRISPR screens enable the exploration of mammalian gene function and genetic regulatory networks. However, use of this technology has been limited by reliance on indirect indexing of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs). Here we present direct-capture Perturb-seq, a versatile screening approach in which expressed sgRNAs are sequenced alongside single-cell transcriptomes. Direct-capture Perturb-seq enables detection of multiple distinct sgRNA sequences from individual cells and thus allows pooled single-cell CRISPR screens to be easily paired with combinatorial perturbation libraries that contain dual-guide expression vectors. We demonstrate the utility of this approach for high-throughput investigations of genetic interactions and, leveraging this ability, dissect epistatic interactions between cholesterol biogenesis and DNA repair. Using direct capture Perturb-seq, we also show that targeting individual genes with multiple sgRNAs per cell improves efficacy of CRISPR interference and activation, facilitating the use of compact, highly active CRISPR libraries for single-cell screens. Last, we show that hybridization-based target enrichment permits sensitive, specific sequencing of informative transcripts from single-cell RNA-seq experiments.

papers.title: Rescuing dendritic cell interstitial motility sustains antitumour immunity.
papers.abstract: The dendritic cell (DC)-initiated and sustained cancer immunity cycle is indispensable for effective endogenous and therapeutically mobilized antitumour T cell responses1-8. This necessitates the continuous migration of antigen-carrying DCs from the tumour microenvironment (TME) to the tumour draining lymph nodes (tdLNs)7-13. Here, through longitudinal analysis of human and mouse tumours, we observed a progressive decrease in migratory conventional DCs (mig-cDCs) in the tdLNs during tumour progression. This decline compromised tumour-specific T cell priming and subsequent T cell supply to the TME. Using a genome-wide in vivo CRISPR screen, we identified phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) and its substrate cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) as key modulators of DC migration. Advanced tumours disrupted cGMP synthesis in DCs to decrease their motility, while PDE5 perturbation preserved the cGMP pool to restore DC migration. Mechanistically, cGMP enhanced myosin-II activity through Rho-associated factors, extending the paradigm of cGMP-regulated amoeboid migration from Dictyostelium to mammalian immune cells. Pharmacological inhibition of PDE5 using sildenafil restored mig-cDC homing to late-stage tdLNs and sustained antitumour immunity in a DC-dependent manner. Our findings bridge fundamental DC interstitial motility to antitumour immunity, revealing that its disruption in chaotic TME promotes immune evasion, and its enhancement offers a promising direction for DC-centric immunotherapy.

papers.title: Single-cell perturbations decipher ribosomal stress-surveillance regulators in type 2 diabetes.
papers.abstract: Systemic characterization of genes and pathways underlying the genetic architecture of type 2 diabetes (T2D) requires scalable functional genomics approaches. Molecular readouts from CRISPR perturbations can effectively uncover the mechanistic effects of underexplored genes. Here we performed single-cell RNA sequencing on pooled CRISPR screens (Perturb-seq) of 61 T2D-associated genes and 40 ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) genes in human pancreatic β cells (EndoC-βH1) for investigations of insulin production and T2D pathology. We identified 21 functional genes, including the uncharacterized KLHL42 and ZZEF1. Findings from global and β cell-specific knockout male mice, islet organoids and human islets reveal that ZZEF1 is a regulator of insulin synthesis and β cell stress through ribosomal stress-surveillance pathways in working and stress status-defined β cell subtypes. ZZEF1 deficiency impairs β cell function by inhibiting the RQC sensor EDF1, which could be improved by azoramide and ISRIB treatments. These Perturb-seq analyses and identification of functional RQC-related genes can provide potential therapeutic targets for T2D.

Prefer rules that help classify likely driver vs reactive vs artifact/confounded vs uncertain.
playbook_context.context_text:
Assay limitations / confounders
- Dissociation / handling stress can drive immediate‑early genes and HSPs; interferon signatures often reflect dissociation, ambient RNA or viral vectors; mitochondrial (MT) gene inflation commonly indicates dying/low‑quality cells rather than biology of interest. (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ; 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md )
- Perturb‑seq specific: strong fitness/selection effects (growth slowdown, sgRNA dropout) and p53/DDR induction are frequent artifacts—these produce cell‑cycle, apoptosis and mitochondrial signals that reflect viability not target biology. (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md )
- Composition shifts (relative expansion/loss of cell types) create pathway enrichment driven by marker genes rather than within‑cell regulation; pooled DE can hide this. Always check per‑cell‑type changes. (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md )

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Cross‑layer concordance = higher confidence: chromatin (ATAC/motifs) + matching RNA changes + protein/activity evidence gives strongest support for a driver; single‑layer RNA alone is weaker and may be reactive. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md )
- Perturb‑seq rule of thumb: if a perturbation reduces cell counts, causes sgRNA dropout, induces p53/DDR or cell‑cycle arrest, treat enriched DDR/cell‑cycle/mito signatures as viability/selection artifacts unless additional evidence opposes this. (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md )
- Growth‑axis disambiguation: mTOR/ribosome/cell‑cycle signatures are likely drivers only when the phenotype implies growth (e.g., proliferation, hypertrophy); otherwise treat them as reactive/selection confounders. Require multiple growth‑layers to agree to call causal. (03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md )
- Operational checklist to call a pathway likely causal (driver): consistent effect across independent guides/replicates, present within (not only across) affected cell types, dose/perturbation‑strength dependence, orthogonal perturbation or inhibition suppresses phenotype, and independent layer support (protein/flux). Absent these, label reactive or uncertain. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md )
- Practical red flags → artifact: isolated MT‑gene enrichment without within‑cell‑type support, immediate‑early/IFN signatures after transduction, single‑guide effect with no replicate concordance. (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ; 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md )

Tissue or cell‑type priors (mouse context)
- Muscle (skeletal/cardiac): high baseline mitochondrial / OXPHOS and mitochondrial biogenesis programs are plausible; mitochondrial enrichment here is more likely biologically meaningful. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md )
- Brain / neurons: mitochondria and oxidative phosphorylation are plausible high‑baseline programs (expect neuron‑specific mitochondrial signatures). (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md )
- Immune cells: metabolic switching (glycolysis vs OXPHOS) is common; IFN/antiviral programs plausible in immune contexts — otherwise treat IFN as potential artifact. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md )
- Tumor / proliferative cells: DDR, p53 and cell‑cycle programs are plausible drivers; in non‑proliferative primary cells these are more likely stress/viability responses. Use tissue prior to set baseline plausibility. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md )

Follow‑up experiments and controls (compact, prioritized)
- Core rule: every candidate program needs ≥1 functional perturbation and ≥1 orthogonal readout; if pathway inhibition removes the phenotype, it likely is causal. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md )
- Mitochondria / OXPHOS: acute functional tests — oligomycin, FCCP; readouts OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), ATP, ROS, and membrane potential; compare with mitochondrial mass/mtDNA and per‑cell‑type expression to exclude dying‑cell artifact. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md ; 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md )
- UPR / proteostasis: validate with UPR markers (ATF4, CHOP) and proteostasis readouts (e.g., ubiquitinated protein levels, proteasome activity assays) and test sensitivity to proteasome modulators; use orthogonal protein assays because RNA alone cannot prove proteasome flux. (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md )
- DDR / apoptosis: γH2AX, Annexin V, caspase activity; test with caspase inhibitors and DNA‑damage agents to see modulation direction. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md )
- Controls specific to perturb‑seq: include multiple independent sgRNAs per gene, non‑targeting controls, measure sgRNA dropout/fitness, compare CRISPRi (or CRISPRa) where possible, and perform per‑cell‑type DE (not only pooled) plus orthogonal cell‑type quantitation (flow cytometry). (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md ; 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md )
- Timecourse and dose: use early timepoints to separate primary (driver) transcriptional responses from secondary reactive programs; test perturbation strength (KO vs partial knockdown) for dose dependence. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md )

gpt.raw_text:
Key observations and interpretation

- Strong OXPHOS enrichment with broad ETC coverage is present. However, state composition differs by perturbation (examples: Cebpa cells Car1 47.8% and Hba‑a2 46.4% vs CTRL Car1 43.7% and Hba‑a2 35.5; Flt3 cells Gstm1 23.0% vs CTRL 10.9; Fcgr3 cells unassigned 23.4% vs CTRL 7.1). This raises the likelihood that pooled OXPHOS signals are reactive/composition‑driven rather than primary target effects.
- Proteasome/UPR signatures co‑enrich with DNA replication/cell‑cycle terms—typical of growth/fitness selection in pooled CRISPR. Treat as reactive pending flux‑level validation.
- DDR/p53 checkpoint terms are enriched at moderate levels and, per Perturb‑seq playbook, likely reflect CRISPR editing/viability artifacts unless guide‑concordant and supported by orthogonal DDR markers.
- Cell‑cycle programs (flagged as possible artifacts) probably reflect selection and state mixing rather than causal proliferation changes.
- Low‑level NF‑κB/innate antiviral signals are uncertain; dissociation or vector can mimic these in immune settings.

What would increase confidence

- Within‑state replication of signatures across independent guides and early timepoints.
- Concordant functional readouts (e.g., OCR/ECAR for OXPHOS; proteasome activity and poly‑Ub for proteostasis; γH2AX/p53 for DDR).
- Fitness/sgRNA‑dropout correlations to flag selection‑driven artifacts.

Actionable validation assays (examples)

- OXPHOS: within‑state GSVA; Seahorse OCR/ECAR; TMRE/ATP; oligomycin/FCCP controls.
- Proteostasis: fluorogenic proteasome activity; poly‑Ub western/flow; MG132 controls.
- DDR/p53: γH2AX foci; p53/p21; p53 inhibition or Trp53 KO dependency.
- Cell cycle: EdU/BrdU and DNA content; guide dropout tracking.
- NF‑κB/innate: early ISG kinetics, p65 nuclear translocation; vector‑only and poly(I:C)/R848 controls.

Caveats

- scRNA‑seq captures RNA only and is sensitive to ambient RNA and dissociation stress.
- Pooled Perturb‑seq frequently shows viability/selection artifacts; per‑state analyses are essential to avoid composition‑driven misattribution.

parsed.headline: OXPHOS and proteostasis programs are strongly enriched in mouse Perturb‑seq data, but patterns and playbook red flags indicate composition and viability/DDR confounding rather than primary target biology.
parsed.executive_summary: Across pooled CRISPR Perturb‑seq in mouse hematopoietic cells, the top signals are mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and proteasome/UPR-proteostasis, with additional DNA-damage/p53 and cell‑cycle terms. Given Perturb‑seq red flags and clear shifts in lineage-state composition across perturbations (for example, Cebpa cells: Car1 47.8% and Hba‑a2 46.4% vs CTRL Car1 43.7% and Hba‑a2 35.5; Flt3 cells: Gstm1 23.0% vs CTRL 10.9; Fcgr3 cells: unassigned 23.4% vs CTRL 7.1), these enrichments are more consistent with reactive or confounded responses than primary causal mechanisms. Low-level NF‑κB/antiviral terms are present but remain uncertain and could reflect dissociation or vector-related innate signaling. Follow-up should prioritize per‑state differential analysis, independent-guide concordance, fitness/sgRNA-dropout checks, and orthogonal functional assays (mitochondrial flux, proteasome activity, DDR markers) to separate driver biology from selection- and composition-driven artifacts.

parsed.markdown_report:
Key observations and interpretation

- Strong OXPHOS enrichment with broad ETC coverage is present. However, state composition differs by perturbation (examples: Cebpa cells Car1 47.8% and Hba‑a2 46.4% vs CTRL Car1 43.7% and Hba‑a2 35.5; Flt3 cells Gstm1 23.0% vs CTRL 10.9; Fcgr3 cells unassigned 23.4% vs CTRL 7.1). This raises the likelihood that pooled OXPHOS signals are reactive/composition‑driven rather than primary target effects.
- Proteasome/UPR signatures co‑enrich with DNA replication/cell‑cycle terms—typical of growth/fitness selection in pooled CRISPR. Treat as reactive pending flux‑level validation.
- DDR/p53 checkpoint terms are enriched at moderate levels and, per Perturb‑seq playbook, likely reflect CRISPR editing/viability artifacts unless guide‑concordant and supported by orthogonal DDR markers.
- Cell‑cycle programs (flagged as possible artifacts) probably reflect selection and state mixing rather than causal proliferation changes.
- Low‑level NF‑κB/innate antiviral signals are uncertain; dissociation or vector can mimic these in immune settings.

What would increase confidence

- Within‑state replication of signatures across independent guides and early timepoints.
- Concordant functional readouts (e.g., OCR/ECAR for OXPHOS; proteasome activity and poly‑Ub for proteostasis; γH2AX/p53 for DDR).
- Fitness/sgRNA‑dropout correlations to flag selection‑driven artifacts.

Actionable validation assays (examples)

- OXPHOS: within‑state GSVA; Seahorse OCR/ECAR; TMRE/ATP; oligomycin/FCCP controls.
- Proteostasis: fluorogenic proteasome activity; poly‑Ub western/flow; MG132 controls.
- DDR/p53: γH2AX foci; p53/p21; p53 inhibition or Trp53 KO dependency.
- Cell cycle: EdU/BrdU and DNA content; guide dropout tracking.
- NF‑κB/innate: early ISG kinetics, p65 nuclear translocation; vector‑only and poly(I:C)/R848 controls.

Caveats

- scRNA‑seq captures RNA only and is sensitive to ambient RNA and dissociation stress.
- Pooled Perturb‑seq frequently shows viability/selection artifacts; per‑state analyses are essential to avoid composition‑driven misattribution.

Distinguish this perturbation's state distribution from cross-target comparisons, and do not call a pathway a direct target-gene mechanism when the same signal could be explained by state-composition differences.

papers.title: The dTAG system for immediate and target-specific protein degradation.
papers.abstract: Dissection of complex biological systems requires target-specific control of the function or abundance of proteins. Genetic perturbations are limited by off-target effects, multicomponent complexity, and irreversibility. Most limiting is the requisite delay between modulation to experimental measurement. To enable the immediate and selective control of single protein abundance, we created a chemical biology system that leverages the potency of cell-permeable heterobifunctional degraders. The dTAG system pairs a novel degrader of FKBP12F36V with expression of FKBP12F36V in-frame with a protein of interest. By transgene expression or CRISPR-mediated locus-specific knock-in, we exemplify a generalizable strategy to study the immediate consequence of protein loss. Using dTAG, we observe an unexpected superior antiproliferative effect of pan-BET bromodomain degradation over selective BRD4 degradation, characterize immediate effects of KRASG12V loss on proteomic signaling, and demonstrate rapid degradation in vivo. This technology platform will confer kinetic resolution to biological investigation and provide target validation in the context of drug discovery.

papers.title: Bidirectional epigenetic editing reveals hierarchies in gene regulation.
papers.abstract: CRISPR perturbation methods are limited in their ability to study non-coding elements and genetic interactions. In this study, we developed a system for bidirectional epigenetic editing, called CRISPRai, in which we apply activating (CRISPRa) and repressive (CRISPRi) perturbations to two loci simultaneously in the same cell. We developed CRISPRai Perturb-seq by coupling dual perturbation gRNA detection with single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling study of pooled perturbations in a mixed single-cell population. We applied this platform to study the genetic interaction between two hematopoietic lineage transcription factors, SPI1 and GATA1, and discovered novel characteristics of their co-regulation on downstream target genes, including differences in SPI1 and GATA1 occupancy at genes that are regulated through different modes. We also studied the regulatory landscape of IL2 (interleukin-2) in Jurkat T cells, primary T cells and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells and elucidated mechanisms of enhancer-mediated IL2 gene regulation. CRISPRai facilitates investigation of context-specific genetic interactions, provides new insights into gene regulation and will enable exploration of non-coding disease-associated variants.

papers.title: Combinatorial single-cell CRISPR screens by direct guide RNA capture and targeted sequencing.
papers.abstract: Single-cell CRISPR screens enable the exploration of mammalian gene function and genetic regulatory networks. However, use of this technology has been limited by reliance on indirect indexing of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs). Here we present direct-capture Perturb-seq, a versatile screening approach in which expressed sgRNAs are sequenced alongside single-cell transcriptomes. Direct-capture Perturb-seq enables detection of multiple distinct sgRNA sequences from individual cells and thus allows pooled single-cell CRISPR screens to be easily paired with combinatorial perturbation libraries that contain dual-guide expression vectors. We demonstrate the utility of this approach for high-throughput investigations of genetic interactions and, leveraging this ability, dissect epistatic interactions between cholesterol biogenesis and DNA repair. Using direct capture Perturb-seq, we also show that targeting individual genes with multiple sgRNAs per cell improves efficacy of CRISPR interference and activation, facilitating the use of compact, highly active CRISPR libraries for single-cell screens. Last, we show that hybridization-based target enrichment permits sensitive, specific sequencing of informative transcripts from single-cell RNA-seq experiments.

papers.title: Rescuing dendritic cell interstitial motility sustains antitumour immunity.
papers.abstract: The dendritic cell (DC)-initiated and sustained cancer immunity cycle is indispensable for effective endogenous and therapeutically mobilized antitumour T cell responses1-8. This necessitates the continuous migration of antigen-carrying DCs from the tumour microenvironment (TME) to the tumour draining lymph nodes (tdLNs)7-13. Here, through longitudinal analysis of human and mouse tumours, we observed a progressive decrease in migratory conventional DCs (mig-cDCs) in the tdLNs during tumour progression. This decline compromised tumour-specific T cell priming and subsequent T cell supply to the TME. Using a genome-wide in vivo CRISPR screen, we identified phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) and its substrate cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) as key modulators of DC migration. Advanced tumours disrupted cGMP synthesis in DCs to decrease their motility, while PDE5 perturbation preserved the cGMP pool to restore DC migration. Mechanistically, cGMP enhanced myosin-II activity through Rho-associated factors, extending the paradigm of cGMP-regulated amoeboid migration from Dictyostelium to mammalian immune cells. Pharmacological inhibition of PDE5 using sildenafil restored mig-cDC homing to late-stage tdLNs and sustained antitumour immunity in a DC-dependent manner. Our findings bridge fundamental DC interstitial motility to antitumour immunity, revealing that its disruption in chaotic TME promotes immune evasion, and its enhancement offers a promising direction for DC-centric immunotherapy.

papers.title: Single-cell perturbations decipher ribosomal stress-surveillance regulators in type 2 diabetes.
papers.abstract: Systemic characterization of genes and pathways underlying the genetic architecture of type 2 diabetes (T2D) requires scalable functional genomics approaches. Molecular readouts from CRISPR perturbations can effectively uncover the mechanistic effects of underexplored genes. Here we performed single-cell RNA sequencing on pooled CRISPR screens (Perturb-seq) of 61 T2D-associated genes and 40 ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) genes in human pancreatic β cells (EndoC-βH1) for investigations of insulin production and T2D pathology. We identified 21 functional genes, including the uncharacterized KLHL42 and ZZEF1. Findings from global and β cell-specific knockout male mice, islet organoids and human islets reveal that ZZEF1 is a regulator of insulin synthesis and β cell stress through ribosomal stress-surveillance pathways in working and stress status-defined β cell subtypes. ZZEF1 deficiency impairs β cell function by inhibiting the RQC sensor EDF1, which could be improved by azoramide and ISRIB treatments. These Perturb-seq analyses and identification of functional RQC-related genes can provide potential therapeutic targets for T2D.

playbook_context.context_text:
Assay limitations / confounders
- Dissociation / handling stress can drive immediate‑early genes and HSPs; interferon signatures often reflect dissociation, ambient RNA or viral vectors; mitochondrial (MT) gene inflation commonly indicates dying/low‑quality cells rather than biology of interest. (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md ; 01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md )
- Perturb‑seq specific: strong fitness/selection effects (growth slowdown, sgRNA dropout) and p53/DDR induction are frequent artifacts—these produce cell‑cycle, apoptosis and mitochondrial signals that reflect viability not target biology. (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md )
- Composition shifts (relative expansion/loss of cell types) create pathway enrichment driven by marker genes rather than within‑cell regulation; pooled DE can hide this. Always check per‑cell‑type changes. (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md )

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Cross‑layer concordance = higher confidence: chromatin (ATAC/motifs) + matching RNA changes + protein/activity evidence gives strongest support for a driver; single‑layer RNA alone is weaker and may be reactive. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md )
- Perturb‑seq rule of thumb: if a perturbation reduces cell counts, causes sgRNA dropout, induces p53/DDR or cell‑cycle arrest, treat enriched DDR/cell‑cycle/mito signatures as viability/selection artifacts unless additional evidence opposes this. (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md )
- Growth‑axis disambiguation: mTOR/ribosome/cell‑cycle signatures are likely drivers only when the phenotype implies growth (e.g., proliferation, hypertrophy); otherwise treat them as reactive/selection confounders. Require multiple growth‑layers to agree to call causal. (03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md )
- Operational checklist to call a pathway likely causal (driver): consistent effect across independent guides/replicates, present within (not only across) affected cell types, dose/perturbation‑strength dependence, orthogonal perturbation or inhibition suppresses phenotype, and independent layer support (protein/flux). Absent these, label reactive or uncertain. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md )
- Practical red flags → artifact: isolated MT‑gene enrichment without within‑cell‑type support, immediate‑early/IFN signatures after transduction, single‑guide effect with no replicate concordance. (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ; 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md )

Tissue or cell‑type priors (mouse context)
- Muscle (skeletal/cardiac): high baseline mitochondrial / OXPHOS and mitochondrial biogenesis programs are plausible; mitochondrial enrichment here is more likely biologically meaningful. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md )
- Brain / neurons: mitochondria and oxidative phosphorylation are plausible high‑baseline programs (expect neuron‑specific mitochondrial signatures). (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md )
- Immune cells: metabolic switching (glycolysis vs OXPHOS) is common; IFN/antiviral programs plausible in immune contexts — otherwise treat IFN as potential artifact. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md )
- Tumor / proliferative cells: DDR, p53 and cell‑cycle programs are plausible drivers; in non‑proliferative primary cells these are more likely stress/viability responses. Use tissue prior to set baseline plausibility. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md )

Follow‑up experiments and controls (compact, prioritized)
- Core rule: every candidate program needs ≥1 functional perturbation and ≥1 orthogonal readout; if pathway inhibition removes the phenotype, it likely is causal. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md )
- Mitochondria / OXPHOS: acute functional tests — oligomycin, FCCP; readouts OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), ATP, ROS, and membrane potential; compare with mitochondrial mass/mtDNA and per‑cell‑type expression to exclude dying‑cell artifact. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md ; 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md )
- UPR / proteostasis: validate with UPR markers (ATF4, CHOP) and proteostasis readouts (e.g., ubiquitinated protein levels, proteasome activity assays) and test sensitivity to proteasome modulators; use orthogonal protein assays because RNA alone cannot prove proteasome flux. (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md )
- DDR / apoptosis: γH2AX, Annexin V, caspase activity; test with caspase inhibitors and DNA‑damage agents to see modulation direction. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md )
- Controls specific to perturb‑seq: include multiple independent sgRNAs per gene, non‑targeting controls, measure sgRNA dropout/fitness, compare CRISPRi (or CRISPRa) where possible, and perform per‑cell‑type DE (not only pooled) plus orthogonal cell‑type quantitation (flow cytometry). (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md ; 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md )
- Timecourse and dose: use early timepoints to separate primary (driver) transcriptional responses from secondary reactive programs; test perturbation strength (KO vs partial knockdown) for dose dependence. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md ; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md )

display.headline: OXPHOS and proteostasis programs are strongly enriched in mouse Perturb‑seq data, but patterns and playbook red flags indicate composition and viability/DDR confounding rather than primary target biology.
display.executive_summary: Across pooled CRISPR Perturb‑seq in mouse hematopoietic cells, the top signals are mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and proteasome/UPR-proteostasis, with additional DNA-damage/p53 and cell‑cycle terms. Given Perturb‑seq red flags and clear shifts in lineage-state composition across perturbations (for example, Cebpa cells: Car1 47.8% and Hba‑a2 46.4% vs CTRL Car1 43.7% and Hba‑a2 35.5; Flt3 cells: Gstm1 23.0% vs CTRL 10.9; Fcgr3 cells: unassigned 23.4% vs CTRL 7.1), these enrichments are more consistent with reactive or confounded responses than primary causal mechanisms. Low-level NF‑κB/antiviral terms are present but remain uncertain and could reflect dissociation or vector-related innate signaling. Follow-up should prioritize per‑state differential analysis, independent-guide concordance, fitness/sgRNA-dropout checks, and orthogonal functional assays (mitochondrial flux, proteasome activity, DDR markers) to separate driver biology from selection- and composition-driven artifacts.

scRNA‑seq (3′ capture) is RNA‑only and subject to dropout, ambient RNA, and 3′ UTR biases; it does not directly measure protein or flux.
Perturb‑seq can induce strong fitness/selection; viability effects (p53/DDR, apoptosis, cell‑cycle arrest) often dominate pooled signals.
Dissociation/handling stress and viral transduction can trigger immediate‑early, interferon, heat‑shock, and NF‑κB programs.
Unknown or mixed timepoints obscure separation of primary vs secondary transcriptional responses.
Pooling across heterogeneous lineage states can convert composition changes into apparent pathway enrichment.
display.raw_text:
Key observations and interpretation

- Strong OXPHOS enrichment with broad ETC coverage is present. However, state composition differs by perturbation (examples: Cebpa cells Car1 47.8% and Hba‑a2 46.4% vs CTRL Car1 43.7% and Hba‑a2 35.5; Flt3 cells Gstm1 23.0% vs CTRL 10.9; Fcgr3 cells unassigned 23.4% vs CTRL 7.1). This raises the likelihood that pooled OXPHOS signals are reactive/composition‑driven rather than primary target effects.
- Proteasome/UPR signatures co‑enrich with DNA replication/cell‑cycle terms—typical of growth/fitness selection in pooled CRISPR. Treat as reactive pending flux‑level validation.
- DDR/p53 checkpoint terms are enriched at moderate levels and, per Perturb‑seq playbook, likely reflect CRISPR editing/viability artifacts unless guide‑concordant and supported by orthogonal DDR markers.
- Cell‑cycle programs (flagged as possible artifacts) probably reflect selection and state mixing rather than causal proliferation changes.
- Low‑level NF‑κB/innate antiviral signals are uncertain; dissociation or vector can mimic these in immune settings.

What would increase confidence

- Within‑state replication of signatures across independent guides and early timepoints.
- Concordant functional readouts (e.g., OCR/ECAR for OXPHOS; proteasome activity and poly‑Ub for proteostasis; γH2AX/p53 for DDR).
- Fitness/sgRNA‑dropout correlations to flag selection‑driven artifacts.

Actionable validation assays (examples)

- OXPHOS: within‑state GSVA; Seahorse OCR/ECAR; TMRE/ATP; oligomycin/FCCP controls.
- Proteostasis: fluorogenic proteasome activity; poly‑Ub western/flow; MG132 controls.
- DDR/p53: γH2AX foci; p53/p21; p53 inhibition or Trp53 KO dependency.
- Cell cycle: EdU/BrdU and DNA content; guide dropout tracking.
- NF‑κB/innate: early ISG kinetics, p65 nuclear translocation; vector‑only and poly(I:C)/R848 controls.

Caveats

- scRNA‑seq captures RNA only and is sensitive to ambient RNA and dissociation stress.
- Pooled Perturb‑seq frequently shows viability/selection artifacts; per‑state analyses are essential to avoid composition‑driven misattribution.

papers.title: Identification and targeting of regulators of SARS-CoV-2-host interactions in the airway epithelium.
papers.abstract: The impact of SARS-CoV-2 in the lung has been extensively studied, yet the molecular regulators of host-cell programs hijacked by the virus in distinct human airway epithelial cell populations remain poorly understood. Some of the reasons include overreliance on transcriptomic profiling and use of nonprimary cell systems. Here we report a network-based analysis of single-cell transcriptomic profiles able to identify master regulator (MR) proteins controlling SARS-CoV-2-mediated reprogramming in pathophysiologically relevant human ciliated, secretory, and basal cells. This underscored chromatin remodeling, endosomal sorting, ubiquitin pathways, as well as proviral factors identified by CRISPR assays as components of the viral-host response in these cells. Large-scale drug perturbation screens revealed 11 candidate drugs able to invert the entire MR signature activated by SARS-CoV-2. Leveraging MR analysis and perturbational profiles of human primary cells represents an innovative approach to investigate pathogen-host interactions in multiple airway conditions for drug prioritization.

papers.title: Identification and Targeting of Regulators of SARS-CoV-2-Host Interactions in the Airway Epithelium.
papers.abstract: Although the impact of SARS-CoV-2 in the lung has been extensively studied, the molecular regulators and targets of the host-cell programs hijacked by the virus in distinct human airway epithelial cell populations remain poorly understood. This is in part ascribed to the use of nonprimary cell systems, overreliance on single-cell gene expression profiling that does not ultimately reflect protein activity, and bias toward the downstream effects rather than their mechanistic determinants. Here we address these issues by network-based analysis of single cell transcriptomic profiles of pathophysiologically relevant human adult basal, ciliated and secretory cells to identify master regulator (MR) protein modules controlling their SARS-CoV-2-mediated reprogramming. This uncovered chromatin remodeling, endosomal sorting, ubiquitin pathways, as well as proviral factors identified by CRISPR analyses as components of the host response collectively or selectively activated in these cells. Large-scale perturbation assays, using a clinically relevant drug library, identified 11 drugs able to invert the entire MR signature activated by SARS-CoV-2 in these cell types. Leveraging MR analysis and perturbational profiles of human primary cells represents a novel mechanism-based approach and resource that can be directly generalized to interrogate signatures of other airway conditions for drug prioritization.

playbook_context.context_text:
Assay limitations / confounders
- Mitochondrial (MT) signal often reflects dying/low-quality cells (“mitochondrial inflation”) rather than biology — check QC %MT and viability.  (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)
- Perturb-seq is biased by fitness/selection: sgRNAs that reduce proliferation or survival produce dropout and downstream signatures (p53, cell‑cycle arrest) that look like biology but are viability artifacts.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)
- scRNA dissociation/handling stress induces IEGs and heat‑shock/UPR genes (FOS/JUN/HSPs) and IFN‑response; these mimic true perturbation responses.  (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)
- Bulk/RNA‑seq limitations apply: cell‑cycle, ribosome, MT, and ISG signatures are common reactive/confounder axes (CDK1 and ribosomal genes may reflect growth/selection).  (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md)
- Cas9/transduction itself can trigger IFN/stress — always compare to non‑targeting and transduction controls.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Within‑cell‑type vs composition: signal that occurs inside a defined cell type = more likely regulatory/driver; signal driven by changes in cell‑type proportions = composition artifact. Validate by per‑cell‑type DE.  (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)
- Cross‑layer support increases driver confidence: RNA change + matching chromatin/TF activity/protein/phospho evidence = stronger causal claim. Single‑layer RNA changes are lower confidence.  (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md)
- Growth‑axis rule: if phenotype does not imply proliferation, treat cell‑cycle / ribosome / mTOR signatures as likely reactive or selection artifacts unless multiple growth layers agree (mTOR + ribosome + E2F). Use presence/absence of canonical drivers (MYC, MKI67, CDK1) to adjudicate.  (03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md)
- Concordance across guides/perturbation modalities: repeated DE across independent sgRNAs, CRISPRi/a, or orthogonal perturbations increases likelihood of a true driver; single‑guide signals are uncertain/artifactual.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)
- Gene‑set coherence & breadth: coherent changes across many ETC / OXPHOS genes (Nduf*, Cox*, Uqcrq, Cyc1) support mitochondrial dysfunction as driver; isolated single‑gene change in a broad complex suggests indirect/reactive effect.  (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md)

Tissue or cell‑type priors
- Use tissue priors to evaluate plausibility: mitochondria/OXPHOS are plausible across many tissues (esp. muscle, brain, high‑metabolic cells); cell‑cycle/S‑phase plausible in dividing/tumor/developing cells but suspicious in mature neurons.  (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md)
- Proteostasis / proteasome and UPR are plausible in secretory cells, high‑protein‑turnover tissues, and stressed/diseased contexts; HSPA8 and proteasome hits are more credible in those contexts.  (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md)
- If pathway violates tissue plausibility (e.g., cell‑cycle signature in terminal neurons), treat as composition or artifact until validated.  (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md)

Follow‑up experiments and controls (concise actionable list)
- Orthogonal functional readouts for mitochondria: OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), ATP levels, mitochondrial membrane potential (TMRE/TMRM), ROS assays; perturb with oligomycin/FCCP to test pathway dependence.  (09_followup_experiment_menu.md)
- Rescue / specificity: express sgRNA‑resistant cDNA or use CRISPRi/CRISPRa to confirm directionality; multiple independent sgRNAs and non‑targeting controls required.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)
- Proteostasis / UPR validation: measure ATF4/CHOP, HSP protein levels, proteasome activity assays, and ubiquitinated protein accumulation; use proteasome inhibitor (MG132) or chaperone modulators as perturbations.  (09_followup_experiment_menu.md)
- Distinguish viability vs mechanism: monitor sgRNA dropout, cell counts, apoptosis (Annexin V), p53/γH2AX; repeat key assays in CRISPRi/a or transient knockdown to separate editing toxicity from target biology.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)
- Cell‑type specificity controls: perform per‑cell‑type DE, sort/population‑purified validation (FACS), or single‑cell protein assays to show effect occurs within cell type rather than via composition shift.  (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)

papers.title: Identification and targeting of regulators of SARS-CoV-2-host interactions in the airway epithelium.
papers.abstract: The impact of SARS-CoV-2 in the lung has been extensively studied, yet the molecular regulators of host-cell programs hijacked by the virus in distinct human airway epithelial cell populations remain poorly understood. Some of the reasons include overreliance on transcriptomic profiling and use of nonprimary cell systems. Here we report a network-based analysis of single-cell transcriptomic profiles able to identify master regulator (MR) proteins controlling SARS-CoV-2-mediated reprogramming in pathophysiologically relevant human ciliated, secretory, and basal cells. This underscored chromatin remodeling, endosomal sorting, ubiquitin pathways, as well as proviral factors identified by CRISPR assays as components of the viral-host response in these cells. Large-scale drug perturbation screens revealed 11 candidate drugs able to invert the entire MR signature activated by SARS-CoV-2. Leveraging MR analysis and perturbational profiles of human primary cells represents an innovative approach to investigate pathogen-host interactions in multiple airway conditions for drug prioritization.

papers.title: Identification and Targeting of Regulators of SARS-CoV-2-Host Interactions in the Airway Epithelium.
papers.abstract: Although the impact of SARS-CoV-2 in the lung has been extensively studied, the molecular regulators and targets of the host-cell programs hijacked by the virus in distinct human airway epithelial cell populations remain poorly understood. This is in part ascribed to the use of nonprimary cell systems, overreliance on single-cell gene expression profiling that does not ultimately reflect protein activity, and bias toward the downstream effects rather than their mechanistic determinants. Here we address these issues by network-based analysis of single cell transcriptomic profiles of pathophysiologically relevant human adult basal, ciliated and secretory cells to identify master regulator (MR) protein modules controlling their SARS-CoV-2-mediated reprogramming. This uncovered chromatin remodeling, endosomal sorting, ubiquitin pathways, as well as proviral factors identified by CRISPR analyses as components of the host response collectively or selectively activated in these cells. Large-scale perturbation assays, using a clinically relevant drug library, identified 11 drugs able to invert the entire MR signature activated by SARS-CoV-2 in these cell types. Leveraging MR analysis and perturbational profiles of human primary cells represents a novel mechanism-based approach and resource that can be directly generalized to interrogate signatures of other airway conditions for drug prioritization.

playbook_context.context_text:
Assay limitations / confounders
- Mitochondrial (MT) signal often reflects dying/low-quality cells (“mitochondrial inflation”) rather than biology — check QC %MT and viability.  (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)
- Perturb-seq is biased by fitness/selection: sgRNAs that reduce proliferation or survival produce dropout and downstream signatures (p53, cell‑cycle arrest) that look like biology but are viability artifacts.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)
- scRNA dissociation/handling stress induces IEGs and heat‑shock/UPR genes (FOS/JUN/HSPs) and IFN‑response; these mimic true perturbation responses.  (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)
- Bulk/RNA‑seq limitations apply: cell‑cycle, ribosome, MT, and ISG signatures are common reactive/confounder axes (CDK1 and ribosomal genes may reflect growth/selection).  (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md)
- Cas9/transduction itself can trigger IFN/stress — always compare to non‑targeting and transduction controls.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Within‑cell‑type vs composition: signal that occurs inside a defined cell type = more likely regulatory/driver; signal driven by changes in cell‑type proportions = composition artifact. Validate by per‑cell‑type DE.  (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)
- Cross‑layer support increases driver confidence: RNA change + matching chromatin/TF activity/protein/phospho evidence = stronger causal claim. Single‑layer RNA changes are lower confidence.  (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md)
- Growth‑axis rule: if phenotype does not imply proliferation, treat cell‑cycle / ribosome / mTOR signatures as likely reactive or selection artifacts unless multiple growth layers agree (mTOR + ribosome + E2F). Use presence/absence of canonical drivers (MYC, MKI67, CDK1) to adjudicate.  (03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md)
- Concordance across guides/perturbation modalities: repeated DE across independent sgRNAs, CRISPRi/a, or orthogonal perturbations increases likelihood of a true driver; single‑guide signals are uncertain/artifactual.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)
- Gene‑set coherence & breadth: coherent changes across many ETC / OXPHOS genes (Nduf*, Cox*, Uqcrq, Cyc1) support mitochondrial dysfunction as driver; isolated single‑gene change in a broad complex suggests indirect/reactive effect.  (01_assay_confounders_rnaseq.md)

Tissue or cell‑type priors
- Use tissue priors to evaluate plausibility: mitochondria/OXPHOS are plausible across many tissues (esp. muscle, brain, high‑metabolic cells); cell‑cycle/S‑phase plausible in dividing/tumor/developing cells but suspicious in mature neurons.  (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md)
- Proteostasis / proteasome and UPR are plausible in secretory cells, high‑protein‑turnover tissues, and stressed/diseased contexts; HSPA8 and proteasome hits are more credible in those contexts.  (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md)
- If pathway violates tissue plausibility (e.g., cell‑cycle signature in terminal neurons), treat as composition or artifact until validated.  (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md)

Follow‑up experiments and controls (concise actionable list)
- Orthogonal functional readouts for mitochondria: OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), ATP levels, mitochondrial membrane potential (TMRE/TMRM), ROS assays; perturb with oligomycin/FCCP to test pathway dependence.  (09_followup_experiment_menu.md)
- Rescue / specificity: express sgRNA‑resistant cDNA or use CRISPRi/CRISPRa to confirm directionality; multiple independent sgRNAs and non‑targeting controls required.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)
- Proteostasis / UPR validation: measure ATF4/CHOP, HSP protein levels, proteasome activity assays, and ubiquitinated protein accumulation; use proteasome inhibitor (MG132) or chaperone modulators as perturbations.  (09_followup_experiment_menu.md)
- Distinguish viability vs mechanism: monitor sgRNA dropout, cell counts, apoptosis (Annexin V), p53/γH2AX; repeat key assays in CRISPRi/a or transient knockdown to separate editing toxicity from target biology.  (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)
- Cell‑type specificity controls: perform per‑cell‑type DE, sort/population‑purified validation (FACS), or single‑cell protein assays to show effect occurs within cell type rather than via composition shift.  (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)
- Timecourse and dose: collect early vs late timepoints to separate immediate/direct transcriptional responses from secondary reactive programs; titer perturbation strength to avoid strong viability artifacts.  (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md)

If you want, I can convert these into a short checklist specific to your top programs/genes (MITO_OXPHOS, ETC genes, Hspa8, Cdk1) with the highest‑priority experiments and expected readouts.

display.headline: Perturb-seq (mouse, Giladi dataset) shows strong OXPHOS and proteostasis/cell-cycle enrichment, but composition and growth/viability biases likely explain much of the signal; treat OXPHOS as uncertain pending within-state validation
display.executive_summary: Across 4,500 cells annotated by lineage_state, overall composition was Car1 1,786 cells (39.7%), Hba-a2 1,409 (31.3%), Gstm1 615 (13.7%), and unassigned 485 (10.8%), with minor states ≤1.6%. Controls (CTRL) were Car1 43.7% (655/1,500), Hba-a2 35.5% (532), Gstm1 10.9% (163), unassigned 7.1% (107). Several perturbation groups deviated substantially: Flt3 had higher Gstm1 23.0% (115) and unassigned 17.2% (86); Fcgr3 had unassigned 23.4% (117) and lower Car1 (31.8%); Klf4 had more Gstm1 21.2% (106) and unassigned 13.2% (66) versus CTRL. Enrichment highlights include strong mitochondria/OXPHOS terms (e.g., electron transport and inner membrane), broad proteasome and S-phase/cell-cycle axes, plus DNA-damage/p53. Given the heterogeneous composition and typical Perturb-seq viability/selection artifacts, we treat cell-cycle and translation as likely artifacts/selection responses, proteasome/S-phase and p53 as likely reactive stress responses, and OXPHOS as uncertain pending within-state analyses and orthogonal functional assays. PubMed retrieval was low-quality/background-only and not used for direct support.

If discussing lineage or cell-state composition, report the relevant state names together with their cell counts and percentages where available. Do not merely say that composition shifted. analysis_result.markdown_report:
Summary of interpretation
- Composition: CTRL Car1 43.7%, Hba-a2 35.5%, Gstm1 10.9%, unassigned 7.1%; Flt3 and Fcgr3 show large increases in Gstm1/unassigned. These shifts can generate apparent pathway changes.
- OXPHOS: Strong ETC/OXPHOS enrichment with Nduf*/Cox*/Uqcrq/Cyc1/VDAC genes. Given composition and growth/stress axes, treat as uncertain until confirmed within states and functionally.
- Proteostasis and S-phase: Proteasome + replication terms suggest reactive stress/proliferation common to Perturb-seq viability effects.
- Cell cycle: Broad growth-axis signature (Cdk1/Ccnb1/Mcm/Top2a/Mki67) likely selection artifact.
- DDR/p53: DNA-damage and checkpoint terms likely reflect CRISPR editing stress.
- Translation/ribosome: Likely growth-axis artifact riding with proliferation and composition.

High-priority validation checklist
- Composition control: per-state DE/pseudobulk; composition-matched downsampling; mixed-effects models.
- Mitochondria: Seahorse OCR/ECAR, ATP, TMRE/ROS; oligomycin/FCCP challenge; replicate across ≥2 sgRNAs; include non-targeting and Cas9-only controls.
- Growth/stress: EdU/Ki-67 cell-cycle profiling; sgRNA dropout; MG132 proteasome challenge; γH2AX and p53 assays.

Literature note
- PubMed retrieval was background-only and not directly relevant; no direct-support literature was used for causal claims.

claims.claim: Proteasome/UPR and S-phase/replication programs are likely reactive stress and proliferation responses rather than primary drivers.
claims.rationale: Enrichment of proteasome complex (Psmb8/9, Psmd1/4/9, Psma1, Psmc4, Psmb2) alongside S-phase, G1/S, replication origin switching and DNA synthesis terms, plus Hspa8 chaperone involvement, is typical of cellular stress and cycling. In Perturb-seq, such axes often reflect viability/selection or transduction/editing stress rather than target-specific regulation.

claims.claim: Mitochondria/OXPHOS transcriptional enrichment is observed but remains uncertain due to composition differences and growth/stress confounding.
claims.rationale: Multiple OXPHOS/ETC terms enriched with coherent complex I/III/IV and VDAC genes (e.g., Ndufv2, Ndufc2, Ndufb3, Ndufa11, Cyc1, Uqcrq, Cox5a, Cox6b2, Vdac1, Chchd2), consistent with metabolic activation. papers.title: Identification and targeting of regulators of SARS-CoV-2-host interactions in the airway epithelium.
papers.abstract: The impact of SARS-CoV-2 in the lung has been extensively studied, yet the molecular regulators of host-cell programs hijacked by the virus in distinct human airway epithelial cell populations remain poorly understood. Some of the reasons include overreliance on transcriptomic profiling and use of nonprimary cell systems. Here we report a network-based analysis of single-cell transcriptomic profiles able to identify master regulator (MR) proteins controlling SARS-CoV-2-mediated reprogramming in pathophysiologically relevant human ciliated, secretory, and basal cells. This underscored chromatin remodeling, endosomal sorting, ubiquitin pathways, as well as proviral factors identified by CRISPR assays as components of the viral-host response in these cells. Large-scale drug perturbation screens revealed 11 candidate drugs able to invert the entire MR signature activated by SARS-CoV-2. Leveraging MR analysis and perturbational profiles of human primary cells represents an innovative approach to investigate pathogen-host interactions in multiple airway conditions for drug prioritization.

papers.title: Identification and Targeting of Regulators of SARS-CoV-2-Host Interactions in the Airway Epithelium.
papers.abstract: Although the impact of SARS-CoV-2 in the lung has been extensively studied, the molecular regulators and targets of the host-cell programs hijacked by the virus in distinct human airway epithelial cell populations remain poorly understood. This is in part ascribed to the use of nonprimary cell systems, overreliance on single-cell gene expression profiling that does not ultimately reflect protein activity, and bias toward the downstream effects rather than their mechanistic determinants. Here we address these issues by network-based analysis of single cell transcriptomic profiles of pathophysiologically relevant human adult basal, ciliated and secretory cells to identify master regulator (MR) protein modules controlling their SARS-CoV-2-mediated reprogramming. This uncovered chromatin remodeling, endosomal sorting, ubiquitin pathways, as well as proviral factors identified by CRISPR analyses as components of the host response collectively or selectively activated in these cells. Large-scale perturbation assays, using a clinically relevant drug library, identified 11 drugs able to invert the entire MR signature activated by SARS-CoV-2 in these cell types. Leveraging MR analysis and perturbational profiles of human primary cells represents a novel mechanism-based approach and resource that can be directly generalized to interrogate signatures of other airway conditions for drug prioritization.

playbook_context.context_text:
Assay limitations / confounders
- Perturb‑seq is strongly biased by fitness/survival effects: sgRNA dropout, slowed growth, p53 / DNA‑damage and cell‑cycle arrest can masquerade as pathway enrichment (treat as viability effects). (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)   
- scRNA‑seq-specific artifacts: dissociation stress (FOS/JUN/EGR1/HSPs), interferon signatures (IFIT/ISG), high mitochondrial reads (apoptotic/low‑quality cells), and cell‑type composition shifts can drive spurious enrichment. Check whether the signal is within‑cell‑type vs driven by marker genes. (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)   
- Layer mismatch: RNA changes alone may reflect downstream transcriptional output (or post‑transcriptional effects); chromatin/TF evidence would indicate regulatory causality — absence of cross‑layer support lowers mechanistic confidence. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md) 

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Fitness/viability triage: if perturbation reduces cell number, induces p53, or causes cell‑cycle arrest → treat enrichment as likely viability/selection artifact unless orthogonal data show pathway specificity. (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)   
- Cross‑layer agreement increases driver confidence: best evidence = (TF motif/accessibility) + (RNA changes of targets) + (protein/activity readout). Single‑layer hits (RNA‑only or ATAC‑only) are lower confidence and may be reactive. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md)   
- Multi‑layer / multi‑component concordance for growth/mitochondrial/proteostasis programs: require agreement across the program (e.g., OXPHOS genes + mitochondrial membrane potential / OCR changes) — single gene/set enrichment without functional change → likely reactive/confounded. (03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md)    
- Practical disambiguation checklist: (1) Is the pathway plausible for the cell type? (2) Does enrichment persist within a defined cell type (not explained by composition)? (3) Do orthogonal perturbations or inhibitors ablate the phenotype? If yes to all → likely driver; if no or mixed → reactive/uncertain. (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md; 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md)   

Tissue or cell‑type priors
- Use tissue plausibility to downweight unexpected programs: e.g., mitochondrial programs are plausible across many cell types (and especially neurons/muscle), whereas immune/IFN programs are suspect in non‑immune contexts. If a pathway violates tissue priors, treat as composition change, developmental artifact, or mapping noise until validated. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md)   
- For scRNA perturbations: always ask whether proteasome/UPR or mitochondrial OXPHOS enrichment maps to known high‑expression cell types (e.g., oxidative tissues, secretory cells). If enrichment is driven by marker genes of a minor cell population → composition artifact. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md; 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)  

Follow‑up experiments and controls (compact, playbook‑recommended)
- Core rule: every enriched program needs ≥1 functional perturbation and ≥1 orthogonal readout; if inhibiting the pathway removes the phenotype → likely causal. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md)   
- Perturb‑seq controls: include non‑targeting sgRNAs, monitor sgRNA dropout / cell counts, and compare CRISPRi/a when possible to separate cutting/DDR effects from on‑target biology. (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)   
- Mitochondrial follow‑ups (for MITO_OXPHOS hits): perturbations such as oligomycin or FCCP; readouts: OCR/ECAR, ATP, ROS, and membrane potential — loss of transcriptional phenotype after perturbation argues for causal OXPHOS involvement. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md)   
- Proteostasis/UPR / proteasome follow‑ups (playbook approach): apply a pathway‑specific perturbation (e.g., proteasome inhibition or genetic modulation) plus orthogonal protein‑level readouts (proteasome activity assays, ubiquitinated protein accumulation, canonical UPR markers) and test whether phenotype depends on proteostasis perturbation — follow the core functional + orthogonal rule. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md; 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md)    
- Validation hierarchy: (a) within‑cell‑type DE and timecourse to establish directionality; (b) pathway inhibition/rescue to test causality; (c) orthogonal protein/functional assays (phospho, activity, imaging). (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md)  

If you want, I can: (A) map these rules onto your specific enrichment hits (proteasome + UPR + MITO_OXPHOS + listed genes) and flag which look more likely driver vs reactive given perturb‑seq confounders and tissue priors, or (B) produce a short experimental plan (exact perturbations, assays, controls) tailored to test proteasome vs mitochondrial causality.

Key signals and interpretation

- A mitochondrial OXPHOS module is also enriched (mitochondrial inner membrane/envelope/membrane; genes Ndufs1/Ndufs7/Sdhb/Vdac1/Cox6b2). This may reflect generic metabolic stress or composition (state-specific mitochondrial baselines) rather than target-specific rewiring.
- DNA-damage/p53 checkpoint and S-phase replication terms (e.g., p53-dependent checkpoints, DNA replication pre-initiation) likely arise from CRISPR cutting–induced growth arrest; several terms were flagged as possible artifacts.
- A modest interferon/stress-granule helicase signature is present at low intensity, typical of scRNA dissociation/culture artifacts.

Cell-state composition matters
- Overall composition (n=4,500): Car1 1,786 (39.7%), Hba-a2 1,409 (31.3%), Gstm1 615 (13.7%), unassigned 485 (10.8%), others <2% each.
- By group (selected): CTRL Car1 655 (43.7%) and Hba-a2 532 (35.5%); Cebpa Car1 239 (47.8%), Hba-a2 232 (46.4%), Gstm1 15 (3.0%); Flt3 Car1 169 (33.8%), Gstm1 115 (23.0%), Hba-a2 107 (21.4%), unassigned 86 (17.2%); Fcgr3 unassigned 117 (23.4%), Hba-a2 111 (22.2%), Car1 159 (31.8%), Pf4 6 (1.2%). These shifts can inflate lineage-tied programs (OXPHOS/proteostasis) if not controlled.

What to do next
- Prioritize within–cell-state DE and a short time-course to establish directionality.
- Functionally probe proteostasis (proteasome inhibitors ± chaperone modulators) and mitochondria (Seahorse ± oligomycin/FCCP) with orthogonal readouts (proteasome activity, XBP1 splicing, OCR/ECAR, ATP, ROS, TMRE).
- Repeat key targets with CRISPRi vs CRISPRn to separate cutting/DDR artifacts from on-target biology; track sgRNA dropout/fitness.
- Include non-targeting controls, QC on mitochondrial reads, and composition matching to deconvolve mixing effects.

Caveat on literature
- External PubMed retrieval for this context was low-quality and provides only background; no direct causal papers aligned with these specific enrichments in this mouse Perturb-seq setting.

parsed.headline: Proteostasis and mitochondrial programs are enriched in mouse Perturb-seq CRISPR responses, but viability and cell-state composition likely confound interpretation
parsed.executive_summary: In a mouse Perturb-seq dataset (4,500 cells; Giladi Perturb-seq), the strongest enrichment involves UPR/proteostasis and proteasome terms (e.g., proteasome complex, protein folding), alongside a mitochondrial OXPHOS module. Cell-cycle/DNA-damage checkpoint signals are also present and flagged as potential artifacts. Interferon/stress-granule features are modest. Cell-state composition differs across perturbation groups (e.g., Cebpa and Flt3), which can drive apparent pathway enrichment. Given scRNA-specific and CRISPR viability confounders, these signals are most consistent with reactive or composition-driven responses rather than primary on-target causality. Within–cell-state analyses, orthogonal functional assays (proteasome and mitochondrial activity), and CRISPRi vs CRISPRn controls are recommended before inferring mechanisms.

claims.claim: Proteasome and protein-folding chaperone programs are prominently enriched and are most consistent with a reactive proteostasis/UPR response to perturbation stress rather than a primary driver mechanism.
claims.rationale: Multiple concordant proteostasis terms with high overlap (proteasome complex, proteasome accessory complex, protein folding, unfolded protein binding, ATP-dependent chaperones) and broad gene support (Psmc/Psmd/Psma subunits, HSP chaperones, Xbp1). In Perturb-seq, proteostasis signatures often arise from generic stress, viability selection, or cutting-induced responses rather than target-specific causality. External PubMed retrieval was low-quality and only background; no direct causal literature for this specific system was found.
confounders: CRISPR cutting–induced stress/viability selection
dissociation stress (HSPs) in scRNA-seq
cell-cycle coupling to proteostasis
cell-state composition differences (e.g., Car1/Hba-a2 vs Gstm1 proportions)
layer mismatch (RNA vs protein activity)

Key signals and interpretation
- UPR/proteostasis and proteasome terms are the top signals (e.g., proteasome complex, protein folding, unfolded protein binding; genes include Psmc/Psmd/Psma subunits, Hsp90ab1/Hspa8/Xbp1). Given Perturb-seq stress and viability confounders, this pattern is most consistent with a reactive proteostasis response, not a primary driver.
- A mitochondrial OXPHOS module is also enriched (mitochondrial inner membrane/envelope/membrane; genes Ndufs1/Ndufs7/Sdhb/Vdac1/Cox6b2). This may reflect generic metabolic stress or composition (state-specific mitochondrial baselines) rather than target-specific rewiring.
- DNA-damage/p53 checkpoint and S-phase replication terms (e.g., p53-dependent checkpoints, DNA replication pre-initiation) likely arise from CRISPR cutting–induced growth arrest; several terms were flagged as possible artifacts.
- A modest interferon/stress-granule helicase signature is present at low intensity, typical of scRNA dissociation/culture artifacts.

Cell-state composition matters
- Overall composition (n=4,500): Car1 1,786 (39.7%), Hba-a2 1,409 (31.3%), Gstm1 615 (13.7%), unassigned 485 (10.8%), others <2% each.
- By group (selected): CTRL Car1 655 (43.7%) and Hba-a2 532 (35.5%); Cebpa Car1 239 (47.8%), Hba-a2 232 (46.4%), Gstm1 15 (3.0%); Flt3 Car1 169 (33.8%), Gstm1 115 (23.0%), Hba-a2 107 (21.4%), unassigned 86 (17.2%); Fcgr3 unassigned 117 (23.4%), Hba-a2 111 (22.2%), Car1 159 (31.8%), Pf4 6 (1.2%). These shifts can inflate lineage-tied programs (OXPHOS/proteostasis) if not controlled.

What to do next
- Prioritize within–cell-state DE and a short time-course to establish directionality.
- Functionally probe proteostasis (proteasome inhibitors ± chaperone modulators) and mitochondria (Seahorse ± oligomycin/FCCP) with orthogonal readouts (proteasome activity, XBP1 splicing, OCR/ECAR, ATP, ROS, TMRE).
- Repeat key targets with CRISPRi vs CRISPRn to separate cutting/DDR artifacts from on-target biology; track sgRNA dropout/fitness.
- Include non-targeting controls, QC on mitochondrial reads, and composition matching to deconvolve mixing effects.

Caveat on literature
- External PubMed retrieval for this context was low-quality and provides only background; no direct causal papers aligned with these specific enrichments in this mouse Perturb-seq setting.

papers.title: Identification and targeting of regulators of SARS-CoV-2-host interactions in the airway epithelium.
papers.abstract: The impact of SARS-CoV-2 in the lung has been extensively studied, yet the molecular regulators of host-cell programs hijacked by the virus in distinct human airway epithelial cell populations remain poorly understood. Some of the reasons include overreliance on transcriptomic profiling and use of nonprimary cell systems. Here we report a network-based analysis of single-cell transcriptomic profiles able to identify master regulator (MR) proteins controlling SARS-CoV-2-mediated reprogramming in pathophysiologically relevant human ciliated, secretory, and basal cells. This underscored chromatin remodeling, endosomal sorting, ubiquitin pathways, as well as proviral factors identified by CRISPR assays as components of the viral-host response in these cells. Large-scale drug perturbation screens revealed 11 candidate drugs able to invert the entire MR signature activated by SARS-CoV-2. Leveraging MR analysis and perturbational profiles of human primary cells represents an innovative approach to investigate pathogen-host interactions in multiple airway conditions for drug prioritization.

papers.title: Identification and Targeting of Regulators of SARS-CoV-2-Host Interactions in the Airway Epithelium.
papers.abstract: Although the impact of SARS-CoV-2 in the lung has been extensively studied, the molecular regulators and targets of the host-cell programs hijacked by the virus in distinct human airway epithelial cell populations remain poorly understood. This is in part ascribed to the use of nonprimary cell systems, overreliance on single-cell gene expression profiling that does not ultimately reflect protein activity, and bias toward the downstream effects rather than their mechanistic determinants. Here we address these issues by network-based analysis of single cell transcriptomic profiles of pathophysiologically relevant human adult basal, ciliated and secretory cells to identify master regulator (MR) protein modules controlling their SARS-CoV-2-mediated reprogramming. This uncovered chromatin remodeling, endosomal sorting, ubiquitin pathways, as well as proviral factors identified by CRISPR analyses as components of the host response collectively or selectively activated in these cells. Large-scale perturbation assays, using a clinically relevant drug library, identified 11 drugs able to invert the entire MR signature activated by SARS-CoV-2 in these cell types. Leveraging MR analysis and perturbational profiles of human primary cells represents a novel mechanism-based approach and resource that can be directly generalized to interrogate signatures of other airway conditions for drug prioritization.

playbook_context.context_text:
Assay limitations / confounders
- Perturb‑seq is strongly biased by fitness/survival effects: sgRNA dropout, slowed growth, p53 / DNA‑damage and cell‑cycle arrest can masquerade as pathway enrichment (treat as viability effects). (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)   
- scRNA‑seq-specific artifacts: dissociation stress (FOS/JUN/EGR1/HSPs), interferon signatures (IFIT/ISG), high mitochondrial reads (apoptotic/low‑quality cells), and cell‑type composition shifts can drive spurious enrichment. Check whether the signal is within‑cell‑type vs driven by marker genes. (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)   
- Layer mismatch: RNA changes alone may reflect downstream transcriptional output (or post‑transcriptional effects); chromatin/TF evidence would indicate regulatory causality — absence of cross‑layer support lowers mechanistic confidence. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md) 

Evidence weighting / driver‑vs‑reactive‑vs‑artifact rules
- Fitness/viability triage: if perturbation reduces cell number, induces p53, or causes cell‑cycle arrest → treat enrichment as likely viability/selection artifact unless orthogonal data show pathway specificity. (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)   
- Cross‑layer agreement increases driver confidence: best evidence = (TF motif/accessibility) + (RNA changes of targets) + (protein/activity readout). Single‑layer hits (RNA‑only or ATAC‑only) are lower confidence and may be reactive. (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md)   
- Multi‑layer / multi‑component concordance for growth/mitochondrial/proteostasis programs: require agreement across the program (e.g., OXPHOS genes + mitochondrial membrane potential / OCR changes) — single gene/set enrichment without functional change → likely reactive/confounded. (03_growth_axis_and_overlap_rules.md; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md)    
- Practical disambiguation checklist: (1) Is the pathway plausible for the cell type? (2) Does enrichment persist within a defined cell type (not explained by composition)? (3) Do orthogonal perturbations or inhibitors ablate the phenotype? If yes to all → likely driver; if no or mixed → reactive/uncertain. (02_assay_confounders_scrna.md; 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md)   

Tissue or cell‑type priors
- Use tissue plausibility to downweight unexpected programs: e.g., mitochondrial programs are plausible across many cell types (and especially neurons/muscle), whereas immune/IFN programs are suspect in non‑immune contexts. If a pathway violates tissue priors, treat as composition change, developmental artifact, or mapping noise until validated. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md)   
- For scRNA perturbations: always ask whether proteasome/UPR or mitochondrial OXPHOS enrichment maps to known high‑expression cell types (e.g., oxidative tissues, secretory cells). If enrichment is driven by marker genes of a minor cell population → composition artifact. (08_tissue_celltype_prior_map.md; 02_assay_confounders_scrna.md)  

Follow‑up experiments and controls (compact, playbook‑recommended)
- Core rule: every enriched program needs ≥1 functional perturbation and ≥1 orthogonal readout; if inhibiting the pathway removes the phenotype → likely causal. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md)   
- Perturb‑seq controls: include non‑targeting sgRNAs, monitor sgRNA dropout / cell counts, and compare CRISPRi/a when possible to separate cutting/DDR effects from on‑target biology. (10_assay_confounders_perturbseq.md)   
- Mitochondrial follow‑ups (for MITO_OXPHOS hits): perturbations such as oligomycin or FCCP; readouts: OCR/ECAR, ATP, ROS, and membrane potential — loss of transcriptional phenotype after perturbation argues for causal OXPHOS involvement. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md)   
- Proteostasis/UPR / proteasome follow‑ups (playbook approach): apply a pathway‑specific perturbation (e.g., proteasome inhibition or genetic modulation) plus orthogonal protein‑level readouts (proteasome activity assays, ubiquitinated protein accumulation, canonical UPR markers) and test whether phenotype depends on proteostasis perturbation — follow the core functional + orthogonal rule. (09_followup_experiment_menu.md; 14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md)    
- Validation hierarchy: (a) within‑cell‑type DE and timecourse to establish directionality; (b) pathway inhibition/rescue to test causality; (c) orthogonal protein/functional assays (phospho, activity, imaging). (14_epigenetic_vs_transcriptional_priors.md; 09_followup_experiment_menu.md)  

If you want, I can: (A) map these rules onto your specific enrichment hits (proteasome + UPR + MITO_OXPHOS + listed genes) and flag which look more likely driver vs reactive given perturb‑seq confounders and tissue priors, or (B) produce a short experimental plan (exact perturbations, assays, controls) tailored to test proteasome vs mitochondrial causality.

display.headline: Proteostasis and mitochondrial programs are enriched in mouse Perturb-seq CRISPR responses, but viability and cell-state composition likely confound interpretation
display.executive_summary: In a mouse Perturb-seq dataset (4,500 cells; Giladi Perturb-seq), the strongest enrichment involves UPR/proteostasis and proteasome terms (e.g., proteasome complex, protein folding), alongside a mitochondrial OXPHOS module. Cell-cycle/DNA-damage checkpoint signals are also present and flagged as potential artifacts. Interferon/stress-granule features are modest. Cell-state composition differs across perturbation groups (e.g., Cebpa and Flt3), which can drive apparent pathway enrichment. Given scRNA-specific and CRISPR viability confounders, these signals are most consistent with reactive or composition-driven responses rather than primary on-target causality. Within–cell-state analyses, orthogonal functional assays (proteasome and mitochondrial activity), and CRISPRi vs CRISPRn controls are recommended before inferring mechanisms.

display.main_uncertainties:
Perturb-seq is biased by fitness/survival effects; CRISPR cutting can induce p53/cell-cycle arrest that masquerades as pathway enrichment.
scRNA-seq dissociation and culture stress can induce immediate early genes, HSPs, and interferon signatures.
High mitochondrial read fractions and low-quality/apoptotic cells can drive mitochondrial/OXPHOS enrichments.
Transcriptional changes alone (RNA layer) may not indicate regulatory causality without orthogonal protein/function evidence.
Cell-type/state composition differences can dominate enrichment signals if not controlled within state.

- A mitochondrial OXPHOS module is also enriched (mitochondrial inner membrane/envelope/membrane; genes Ndufs1/Ndufs7/Sdhb/Vdac1/Cox6b2). This may reflect generic metabolic stress or composition (state-specific mitochondrial baselines) rather than target-specific rewiring.
- DNA-damage/p53 checkpoint and S-phase replication terms (e.g., p53-dependent checkpoints, DNA replication pre-initiation) likely arise from CRISPR cutting–induced growth arrest; several terms were flagged as possible artifacts.
- A modest interferon/stress-granule helicase signature is present at low intensity, typical of scRNA dissociation/culture artifacts.

Cell-state composition matters
- Overall composition (n=4,500): Car1 1,786 (39.7%), Hba-a2 1,409 (31.3%), Gstm1 615 (13.7%), unassigned 485 (10.8%), others <2% each.
- By group (selected): CTRL Car1 655 (43.7%) and Hba-a2 532 (35.5%); Cebpa Car1 239 (47.8%), Hba-a2 232 (46.4%), Gstm1 15 (3.0%); Flt3 Car1 169 (33.8%), Gstm1 115 (23.0%), Hba-a2 107 (21.4%), unassigned 86 (17.2%); Fcgr3 unassigned 117 (23.4%), Hba-a2 111 (22.2%), Car1 159 (31.8%), Pf4 6 (1.2%). These shifts can inflate lineage-tied programs (OXPHOS/proteostasis) if not controlled.

What to do next
- Prioritize within–cell-state DE and a short time-course to establish directionality.
- Functionally probe proteostasis (proteasome inhibitors ± chaperone modulators) and mitochondria (Seahorse ± oligomycin/FCCP) with orthogonal readouts (proteasome activity, XBP1 splicing, OCR/ECAR, ATP, ROS, TMRE).
- Repeat key targets with CRISPRi vs CRISPRn to separate cutting/DDR artifacts from on-target biology; track sgRNA dropout/fitness.
- Include non-targeting controls, QC on mitochondrial reads, and composition matching to deconvolve mixing effects.

Caveat on literature
- External PubMed retrieval for this context was low-quality and provides only background; no direct causal papers aligned with these specific enrichments in this mouse Perturb-seq setting.
